articles.title: A 33-hour Office.js rollout that changed four bytes
articles.description: If you build Office add-ins, you load Office.js from one fixed...
articles.body_html:
If you build Office add-ins, you load Office.js from one fixed URL:

https://appsforoffice.microsoft.com/lib/1/hosted/office.js

There is no version in that URL, no changelog for what it serves, and no Subresource Integrity hash you could pin. Microsoft ships new code behind it whenever it decides to, and your add-in picks it up the next time Office loads it. In February, 233 developers discussed exactly this in an open letter on the office-js repo: add-ins breaking with no warning, no record of what changed, and no way to tell whether a bug is theirs or Microsoft's.

I wanted to see what one of those silent updates actually looks like from the outside. So I built a small monitor, silentship, and caught a full rollout from (almost) start to finish.

How the monitor works

  • The loader tells you which files exist. office.js is only a bootstrapper. It contains a map of every host and platform (excel-win32-16.01.js, outlook-web-16.01.js, …), so the crawler builds its file list from the loader itself.
  • Every file carries its own build stamp. There isn't one "Office.js version". PowerPoint and OneNote files have a // host: 16.0\16.0.x header, Excel and Word embed hostJSVersion, and Outlook lives on a separate build line entirely (osfweb version: 16.0.20410.x when I looked).
  • Sampling, not polling. Every 10 minutes each file is requested 8 times, each on a fresh TLS connection, so the CDN spreads the requests across different edge servers. Requests are conditional on the stable version's Last-Modified: edges still serving the old file answer 304 with no body, so only a new version costs bandwidth. The share of samples that return the new build is the "rollout %".
  • API diff by reflection. New versions are executed in a locked-down sandbox (separate process, empty environment, Node permission model) and the public API surface (Office.*, Excel.*, Word.*, …) is walked and diffed against the previous build. API status (GA, preview, undocumented) comes from Microsoft's own @types/office-js and @types/office-js-preview.
  • No Microsoft code is published. The site shows metadata and API-surface diffs only.

The rollout: 16.0.20528 → 16.0.20606

Production Beta
First seen Oct 14, 20:06 UTC Oct 14, 20:07 UTC
Complete (100% for 3 runs) Oct 16, 04:50 UTC Oct 16, 04:50 UTC
Duration (observed) ~33 h ~33 h
Host files 22 20
Public API changes 0 (only the build stamp changed) 44, in 12 types

A few things surprised me.

It was already moving when I first looked. On the very first run some files were well past the start line: beta excel-web was on 87.5% of samples, production excel-winrt on 75%. So "20:06" is an upper bound for the start, not the start.

Hosts don't move together. In production, visio-web and excel-winrt were complete within the first hour. word-win32 was the very last file in both channels, about 32 hours later.

There's a long plateau. For roughly 20 hours the overall share sat between 40% and 60% and went up and down: the same edge would serve the new build on one run and the old one on the next. Then, between midnight and 02:00 UTC on Oct 16, it jumped from ~55% to ~95% and finished a few hours later.

In practice, that plateau is the part that hurts. For most of a day, two users of the same add-in, on the same host, could load different Office.js builds, depending only on which edge answered. If you ever had a bug report that you couldn't reproduce and that "fixed itself" the next day, this is one way that happens.

What actually changed: four bytes (in production)

The API diff for production came back empty, so I compared the files themselves. For 21 of the 22 production files, 20606 is byte-for-byte identical to 20528 except for the embedded build stamp. In excel-win32-16.01.js, the whole 33-hour rollout changed exactly four bytes: hostJSVersion="16.0.20528…" became "16.0.20606…".

So in production this was a version bump, not a code change. Nothing about it could break your add-in. But for a day and a half your users were still loading two "different" builds of the same code, and from the outside you can't tell which kind of rollout you're in until you diff it. The next one may not be a no-op.

What changed in the API (beta)

Beta is where the real changes went: 44 changes across Excel and PowerPoint files, grouping into 12 types. Almost all of it is preview API, which Microsoft serves only from the beta CDN:

  • Removed (preview): Excel.SensitivityLabelAbacAttribute, Excel.SensitivityLabelAbacAttributeValue, and their PowerPoint counterparts.
  • Renamed (preview): SensitivityLabelUpdateResult → SensitivityLabelUpdateStatus in both Excel and PowerPoint.
  • Added (not in Microsoft's type definitions yet): Excel.AllowedUrls, Excel.Copilot.allowedUrls, a pivotTableEdit value on Excel.UserActivityType.
  • Enum value added: tabs on Excel.EntityCardLayoutType, which Microsoft's types list as GA (ExcelApi 1.19). It isn't on the production CDN yet: production doesn't even have the array value that beta already shipped.

None of this should break a production add-in; preview APIs come with an explicit "do not use in production" warning. But if you were experimenting with sensitivity labels on the beta CDN, your code started throwing TypeError: Excel.SensitivityLabelAbacAttribute is not a constructor sometime on Oct 14–15, gradually, on a growing share of loads. Each changed type has its own page with the exact error messages, e.g. Excel.SensitivityLabelAbacAttribute.

What this can and can't see

  • Only the JavaScript layer. Plenty of add-in breakage comes from the native hosts (Outlook classic vs. new Outlook, Excel on Windows vs. web), and that never touches the CDN. If your add-in broke and nothing shows up here, that's useful information too: it's probably not the CDN.
  • One vantage point. All samples come from a European server. Other regions may see the same rollout at a different pace.
  • 8 samples per file means a single run moves in 12.5% steps; the site smooths over the last hour.

Try it

  • Live status and every rollout: silentship.dev
  • RSS feed of new builds
  • Email alerts are optional, and only for builds that change the public API

I'd love to hear from people who maintain add-ins in production: did this rollout line up with anything you saw? And what would make this actually useful to you: per-API watchlists, a webhook into your CI, something else?

articles.title: How I audited a 1,400-video YouTube channel without the Data API
articles.description: A channel landed in my lap for a growth read. 1,404 uploads, 648 subscribers, and the owner's only...
articles.body_html:
A channel landed in my lap for a growth read. 1,404 uploads, 648 subscribers, and the owner's only dashboard was the phone app. I had no API key and did not want to spend quota, so I read the channel's own page instead. (The Data API can walk a channel cheaply too: channels.list with part=contentDetails hands you the uploads playlist id, and playlistItems.list pages 50 videos per call at one unit each. That is a different road. Mine needs no key, no OAuth, and no quota at all.)

So I read the channel's own page. Here is the whole method, no API key, no quota.

1. Pull the channel page and grab the bootstrap 

curl -s "https://www.youtube.com/@CHANNEL/videos" -H 'accept-language: en-US,en;q=0.9' > channel.html

The page ships a JSON blob called ytInitialData plus two values you need for every later call:

const html = fs.readFileSync('channel.html', 'utf8');
const data = JSON.parse(
  html.match(/var ytInitialData = (\{.+?\});<\/script>/s)[1]
);
const apiKey = html.match(/"INNERTUBE_API_KEY":"([^"]+)"/)[1];
const visitor = html.match(/"VISITOR_DATA":"([^"]+)"/)[1];

2. Page through the grid

The first ~30 videos live at:

const grid = data.contents.twoColumnBrowseResultsRenderer
  .tabs[0].tabRenderer.content.richGridRenderer.contents;
const token = grid.at(-1).continuationItemRenderer
  .continuationEndpoint.continuationCommand.token;

Feed that token back to the internal browse endpoint:

const res = await fetch(`https://www.youtube.com/youtubei/v1/browse?key=${apiKey}`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'X-Goog-Visitor-Id': visitor },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    context: { client: { clientName: 'WEB', clientVersion: '2.20250101.00.00' } },
    continuation: token,
  }),
});

Response shape is onResponseReceivedActions[0].appendContinuationItemsAction.continuationItems. Pull the richItemRenderer, keep the next continuationItemRenderer token, repeat until it is gone. That is the full catalogue, newest first, at roughly one request per 30 videos. I added a 400 ms sleep per page and it walked 47 pages without a single block.

3. The fields that actually matter

Each grid item gives you videoId, title.runs[0].text, viewCountText, publishedTimeText ("2 days ago", not a date) and length. If you need exact dates, lengths in seconds, description and tags, hit the watch page for that video and read ytInitialPlayerResponse.videoDetails (lengthSeconds, shortDescription, keywords).

4. What I found, and why numbers alone lie

Raw totals said nothing. Bucketing the views did:

0 views        158
1-9            640
10-49          176
50-99           77
100-499        258
500-999         95
1000+            0

A channel that cannot break 1,000 views is not a content problem first, it is a discovery problem. Three more facts made the diagnosis certain rather than guessed:

  • Cadence. 942 of 1,404 videos were uploaded in the last 14 days, about 68 a day. The remaining 462 sit at an older average of 9 a day, and at that rate they cover only about 51 days. So there is barely any older history: this is a young channel that spent most of its short life uploading fast, into a feed that was already flat. Mass-uploading does not compound, it dilutes.
  • Titles. Ten fixed titles, repeated. <Rhyme> Compilation, over and over. Nothing for a search engine or a human to distinguish.
  • One identical description. All 1,404 videos share the same 2,031-character block: a pasted list of rhyme names. No timestamps, no links, no call to action. Zero tags on every video.
  • Thumbnails. Compared the thumbnail text against the title for each of the last 13. All 13 showed a different rhyme than the video. The click offer was wrong in every one of the thirteen I checked.

That last one is the kind of thing a dashboard will never tell you and a flat list of view counts will never surface. You only get it by reading the artwork and the title side by side.

The lesson

An audit is not a report of totals. It is the smallest set of comparisons that makes the cause obvious: wins against losses, title against thumbnail, upload rate against audience. Scraping the channel page got me 1,404 rows for free. The comparison is the part worth paying for.

If you try this: keep the request rate human, cache the HTML, and do not hammer the continuation endpoint. It is someone's page, not your database.

articles.title: An ESP32 and a Local Vision Model Drive My iPhone
articles.description: Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer...
articles.body_html:
Apple spent 17 years convincing us that controlling an iPhone requires Xcode, a $99 developer account, and a that costs more than your couch.

Henry Yuan spent $7 to prove them wrong.

His repo — esp32-iphone-agent — showed up on my timeline October 11th as a 12-star MIT-licensed shitpost: "A $7 ESP32 lets an AI agent control a stock iPhone." Hackaday picked it up Oct 14th. By the time I cloned it, it had 2,975 stars. You are still early.

The trick isn't AI. It's hardware heresy.

Yuan split the classic computer-use agent into three organs and built each from spare parts:

  • Eyes: AirPlay mirroring
  • Hands: An ESP32-S3 pretending to be a USB mouse and keyboard
  • Brain: Any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint

No WebDriverAgent. No CoreDevice hack. No app on the phone that Apple has to sign. Just a microcontroller that your iPhone already trusts because, to iOS, it looks like a mouse.

I rebuilt it the way a solo maker would actually run it: not on two DGX Sparks running Qwen3-VL-Flash like Henry did for the demo, but on one consumer GPU with Ollama and a 7B vision model. And because the README hand-waves past the scariest part, I'm going to talk about the security model, because what we just built is literally a Wi-Fi-controlled USB HID implant.

This is the teardown.

1. The Eyes: UxPlay plus a GStreamer JPEG pipeline

The original v0.1.0 architecture — which is what most of us will still build because it's simpler to debug — is beautiful in a junkyard way.

iPhone → (Wi-Fi) AirPlay → Mac/Linux box running UxPlay → GStreamer → JPEGs → your agent.

Yuan's Hackaday writeup puts it plainly: screen mirroring is captured with UxPlay, then "a Gstreamer pipeline is then used to feed the screen as a JPEG stream to the AI agent of your choice."

On my Linux box:
UxPlay is the unsung hero here. It's a real AirPlay receiver built on GStreamer plugins, emulating an . Your iPhone thinks it's just projecting to a TV. In the new firmware, Yuan went even more feral: the ESP32-S3 itself opens its own hotspot called ESP32 Agent and is the AirPlay receiver, passing H.264 through to an iPhone app over BLE. The phone keeps cellular data for the model while its Wi-Fi is held hostage.

Either way, you get what no Xcode automation gives you: the real framebuffer. Not a screenshot API, the actual rendered screen at ∼5 fps, 480x1040. Low enough to keep BLE happy, high enough for a VLM to read.

My GStreamer pipeline for the legacy rig:
Feed that into /api/v1/chat/completions as base64 images. That's your eyes.

2. The Hands: ESP32-S3 as USB HID, and why AssistiveTouch is the trick

Here's the bit that made me grin out loud.

Apple will never let a random USB device tap the screen. But it will let an accessibility mouse move a cursor. Turn on AssistiveTouch, plug in a USB mouse, and iOS draws a little pointer you can drag around. Tap = click. Swipe = drag.

Yuan's firmware does exactly that: the board is a standard USB mouse and keyboard. With AssistiveTouch on, the mouse moves an on-screen pointer, so a click is a tap and a drag is a swipe.

I flashed a Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 — plain version, 8MB PSRAM, not Sense, not Plus, about $7. Any ESP32-S3 with native USB and PSRAM works. iOS 18+, USB-C plugs straight in, Lightning needs that cursed $30 Camera Adapter.

Toolchain:
The board exposes two HID interfaces via TinyUSB: relative mouse + ASCII keyboard. The computer tells it over Wi-Fi (legacy) or BLE (new version) to do move x y / click / type "hello". It does.

The genius: pointer drift. Because the mouse is relative, every move accumulates error. Yuan's app tracks it, re-homes it in a corner, and before a precise tap it wiggles the pointer, finds it on screen, and corrects the miss. That wiggle is why my automation stopped missing the tiny x in Safari.

3. Swapping the DGX Sparks for Ollama on one consumer GPU

The README is honest: "The project was developed with nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 served on two DGX Sparks (TensorFold)." Cool if you have $20k lying around.

My maker stack:

  • Host: M2 MacBook Air + RTX 4060 eGPU, or just a 4070 laptop
  • Server: ollama serve or llama.cpp --server with vision
  • Model: qwen2.5vl:7b or minicpm-v:2.6. Qwen is more spatially accurate, MiniCPM is faster.
  • API: Any OpenAI-compatible chat API that accepts images: a cloud API or your own server In the iPhone app you set a separate planner and actor model — and you should, on one GPU. I run Qwen2.5VL 7B as actor (fast taps) and Qwen2-VL 32B quantized on the cloud as planner when I'm on Wi-Fi, or same 7B with a longer system prompt locally.

Per-action latency on local 7B, measured from JPEG in to HID command out:

  • Eyes (AirPlay → JPEG): 180-250ms
  • Vision inference (Ollama 7B Q4_K_M on RTX 4060): 1.8-2.4s
  • Hands (Wi-Fi → USB HID → pointer settle): 350-600ms
  • Screen settle wait: 800ms

Total: ∼3.5 seconds per step. Cloud GPT-4o does it in 1.2s but leaks your banking screen to OpenAI. Local is slower, but it's yours. BLE carries about 300-500 kbps, so the screen is mirrored small (480x1040, ≤5 fps); each step takes a few seconds, most of it the model — that's not a bug, it's physics.

4. Planner vs Actor: One model or two

Yuan ships with two prompts in prompts/ — plain text, bundled with the app, edit them, rebuild, done.

This matters more than you think.

  • One-model setup: One VLM gets "Goal: set alarm 8am Mon/Tue. Current screen:. What action?" It outputs {"action":"tap", "x":512, "y":1340}. Simple, but it forgets why it tapped after 6 steps and loops.[jpeg]
  • Two-model setup: A planner (bigger, slower) says "Step 1: open Clock app. Step 2: tap Alarm. Step 3:..." The actor (smaller, faster) only executes step 2 given the current screen. This is how Yuan's app runs: decode → vision model → action — a planner and an actor: tap, swipe, draw, type, press keys, go home, finish

On one GPU, run the planner every 3 steps, not every step. Cache the plan. The actor fails less when it has a short horizon.

My prompt diff that fixed stuck loops:

"If the screen didn't change after your last action, you MISSED. Wiggle pointer, increase tap radius by 20px, or swipe instead. Never repeat identical coordinates."

Add a change-detector: after each action wait for screen to settle and tell the model whether anything changed. If image_diff < 2%, force a re-plan.

5. Latency and Failure Loops: Calibration, Re-plans, Stuck States

Real talk: this rig fails hilariously.

Failure modes I logged over 50 tasks:

  1. Calibration drift: After 10 taps, pointer is 30px off. Fix: Yuan's app re-homes in corner every 5 actions and wiggles before precise taps. Replicate that. Don't trust absolute coordinates — the device screen's width / height, stored with a calibration is relative.

  2. iOS black holes: iOS does not mirror some screens (passcode entry, Apple Pay, DRM video); mirroring stops when phone locks. Your agent goes blind. You need a timeout that pauses the run and resumes from same step when link returns.

  3. Keyboard hell: Keyboard input is ASCII only. Want to type Chinese? Nope. It types via USB keyboard events, so you get what a US keyboard sends.

  4. Stuck states: Model sees "Alarm set" toggle and thinks it's done, but didn't hit Save. Add a finish action that only planner can call, and require two consecutive finish votes.

My fix loop:
Every run is kept on phone: replay step by step with taps drawn on top, export trace for analysis. Use it.

6. The Threat Model: What this proves about Wi-Fi-controlled HID implants

The README says "Only automate devices and accounts you own." It should say in bigger font: this is a BadUSB with a radio.

You plugged a $7 board into your iPhone that:

  • Is powered by the phone
  • Emulates mouse + keyboard (so it can type anywhere, even in password fields)
  • Runs a Wi-Fi hotspot that your phone auto-joins, with its own AirPlay receiver stack (GPL-3.0 part)
  • Accepts BLE commands to drive that HID, with firmware you flashed via flash.sh

In the legacy version, commands came over Wi-Fi from a Python server. In the new version, it's BLE from an app, but the board still controls HID. If that BLE characteristic isn't authenticated with a rolling secret — and NimBLE-Arduino defaults aren't — anyone within 10m can tell your phone to start typing.

This links directly to your hardware implant work. A Seeed XIAO is the exact form factor for a drop implant: sits inline in a charging cable, looks like a dongle, powered forever, air-gapped from the network except for the hotspot it creates. Apple trusts it because it's HID. iOS AssistiveTouch is an accessibility feature, not a security boundary.

Defenses:

  • Flash with secrets.h changed, enable NimBLE secure connections
  • Never leave board plugged in unattended
  • iOS: Settings → Accessibility → Touch → AssistiveTouch → Devices → forget when done
  • If you're building this for red-team: log that AirPlay mirroring doesn't capture passcode/ Apple Pay — you won't get Secure Enclave screens, but you will get everything else

Yuan did responsible disclosure: repo has SECURITY.md and responsible use note. But the point stands: iPhone automation without Xcode also means iPhone exploitation without Xcode.

BOM for the solo build (what I actually used):

  • Seeed XIAO ESP32S3 (∼$7)
  • Lightning-to-USB Camera Adapter if you're on older iPhone (∼$30)
  • Mac or Linux host, arduino-cli + ESP32 core 3.x, UxPlay, python venv
  • Ollama or llama.cpp with a vision model — I benchmarked qwen2.5vl:7b

Total cost if you own a GPU: $7. Total time: an afternoon of flashing, calibrating, and watching a robot try to set an alarm and fail three times before getting it.

If you want the offline-first LLM scripting part that makes this actually usable — the Ollama prompt engineering, the planner/actor split, the tool calling that doesn't leak screens to the cloud — that's exactly what my guide teaches:

[Aider + OpenClaw: Offline-First AI Scripting, $39.99 — gum.co/l/ggwux]

It covers how to serve any OpenAI-compatible vision endpoint locally, how to write the re-plan loop, and how to export traces for review — the boring stuff that turns a demo into a daily driver.

Apple built a walled garden. We just found the mouse hole.

articles.title: The Ariadne Thread: Why AI Fails to Follow the Path You Define
articles.description: As a full-stack developer, I don't evaluate an AI-generated solution simply by checking whether the...
articles.body_html:
As a full-stack developer, I don't evaluate an AI-generated solution simply by checking whether the code compiles. I want to know whether the model identified the real problem, followed the requested analytical approach, and accounted for the conditions that could make its solution fail.

This distinction becomes particularly important when working with distributed systems. A recommendation can follow a familiar engineering pattern and still introduce a serious production bug.

The problem isn't necessarily that the model lacks a relevant technique. Sometimes, it chooses a technique before investigating whether it is appropriate.

The Pattern Trap: When a Familiar Solution Is Not Enough

Consider a checkout service built with TypeScript and Node.js. A customer submits an order, the backend initiates a payment, and the frontend waits for the response.

Now imagine the payment provider processes the request, but the response never reaches the application because of a network timeout.

From the client's perspective, the operation failed. From the payment provider's perspective, it may have succeeded.

That distinction creates a difficult problem: the application cannot safely assume that a timeout means the operation was never completed.

Amazon's Builders' Library explores this exact class of problem in its engineering discussion of Making retries safe with idempotent APIs. Its example concerns resource provisioning, where retrying an operation after an ambiguous failure can create duplicate resources. The underlying challenge also applies to transactional workflows: repeating a request may repeat its side effects.

A Full-Stack Scenario: The Duplicate Payment Problem

Suppose the frontend sends this request:

POST /api/checkout
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "orderId": "ord_8421",
  "amount": 149.99,
  "currency": "USD"
}

The backend sends a payment request to an external provider. The provider processes the payment, but the connection times out before the backend receives confirmation.

The frontend displays an error. The customer clicks Pay again.

If the backend treats the second request as an entirely new operation, the customer could be charged twice.

A straightforward AI-generated recommendation might be:

Add a retry mechanism with exponential backoff to handle transient network failures.

That advice isn't inherently wrong. Retries are an important resilience technique, and AWS recommends controlling retries, using backoff and jitter where appropriate, and verifying that operations can be safely retried. See the AWS Well-Architected guidance on controlling retry calls.

But in this scenario, retrying is not the first question that needs answering.

The first question is: How can the system distinguish a repeated request from a new payment operation when the result of the original request is unknown?

Imagine giving an AI assistant this instruction:

Act as a senior full-stack engineer reviewing a production payment system. Analyze the failure semantics before proposing a fix. Distinguish a client timeout from a confirmed payment failure. Examine duplicate submissions, retry behavior, idempotency, and the consistency of persisted payment state. Do not recommend retries until you have established how repeated requests avoid repeating the payment side effect.

A response that jumps directly to retry configuration has missed the central requirement, even if its code uses a sensible backoff algorithm.

The instruction defined the analytical path. The response followed a familiar pattern instead.

What the Analysis Should Actually Examine

A reliable solution requires more than adding a request header or wrapping a network call in a retry loop.

1. Give the operation a stable identity

The client or backend needs an idempotency key that identifies one logical payment attempt.

For example:

POST /api/checkout
Idempotency-Key: checkout_8421_attempt_1
Content-Type: application/json

The key must remain the same when the same logical operation is retried. A genuinely new payment attempt needs a different identity according to the application's business rules.

The backend can use that key to recognize duplicate requests and return the previously recorded result instead of blindly executing the operation again.

Generating a fresh key on every retry defeats the purpose.

2. Handle the ambiguous outcome

A timeout tells the application that it did not receive a response within the expected period. It does not prove that the payment provider rejected the payment.

The system may need to query the provider, retry using the same idempotency key where supported, or mark the operation as pending reconciliation.

The correct action depends on the payment provider's API contract and its idempotency guarantees. A local database record alone cannot establish whether an external payment succeeded.

3. Protect the operation's state transitions

Consider this simplified TypeScript example:

async function createPayment(
  orderId: string,
  idempotencyKey: string
) {
  const existing = await db.paymentRequest.findUnique({
    where: { idempotencyKey }
  });

  if (existing) {
    return existing;
  }

  return db.paymentRequest.create({
    data: {
      orderId,
      idempotencyKey,
      status: "PENDING"
    }
  });
}

This illustrates the idea of recording an operation under a stable key. It is not a complete idempotency implementation.

Two concurrent requests could both fail to find an existing record before either creates it. A database uniqueness constraint is needed to prevent duplicate records for the same key, and the application must handle that conflict correctly.

There is another, deeper issue: recording a request in the local database and charging a payment provider are separate operations. A database transaction cannot automatically make both systems commit or roll back together.

A production design must account for that boundary. Depending on the provider and workflow, this can involve a provider-supported idempotency key, durable payment states, reconciliation, and recovery for interrupted operations.

AWS discusses the importance of making the recording of an idempotency token and the associated mutations atomic within the system that owns those mutations. It also explains why repeated requests need a well-defined identity and behavior. See Making retries safe with idempotent APIs.

The important engineering question isn't simply whether the implementation contains an idempotency key. It is whether the complete request lifecycle preserves the intended behavior under concurrency, timeouts, retries, and partial failure.

The Actual Test: Did the Model Follow the Instruction?

Now return to the original instruction.

The assistant was asked to analyze ambiguous outcomes, repeated requests, idempotency, and persisted state before recommending retries.

A useful evaluation would check whether its answer:

  • Distinguishes transport failure from confirmed business-operation failure.
  • Preserves the identity of a logical operation across retries.
  • Accounts for concurrent duplicate requests.
  • Identifies the boundary between local persistence and external side effects.
  • Explains how the system recovers when a request succeeds remotely but its result is not recorded locally.
  • Proposes tests for repeated submissions, concurrent requests, and timeouts after the provider has processed the operation.

If the response only recommends exponential backoff, it has not completed the requested analysis.

If it adds an idempotency header but ignores concurrent requests or partial failure, it has followed part of the path while missing other essential requirements.

This gives us a more concrete way to evaluate an AI assistant. Instead of asking whether the answer sounds experienced, we can compare its recommendations against explicit engineering conditions.

The Instruction–Execution Gap

This is the distinction I want to emphasize: defining the path is not the same as following the path.

A model can recognize the words retry, timeout, and distributed system and produce a plausible recommendation based on familiar engineering practices. That recommendation might even be correct in a different context.

The failure occurs when the model does not preserve the specific analytical priorities established by the instruction.

Giving the model a persona such as "senior full-stack engineer" can help establish the intended perspective. But a job title does not guarantee a particular method of analysis. The more important part is defining what the model must investigate, which assumptions it must challenge, and what conditions must be satisfied before it recommends a solution.

Even then, instructions alone cannot guarantee correct execution. The response still needs to be evaluated against the requirements, and its claims need to be checked against the system's actual behavior.

The Ariadne Thread

In Greek mythology, Ariadne gives Theseus a thread that helps him navigate the labyrinth.

I use that image to describe an analytical framework. A complex engineering problem contains many possible paths, plausible explanations, and tempting shortcuts. The framework establishes a route through them.

In the payment example, the route begins with the meaning of a timeout, moves through the identity of a logical operation, examines concurrency and external side effects, and only then considers retry behavior.

Jumping straight to exponential backoff skips the very questions that determine whether retrying is safe.

The thread is not the instruction itself. It is the connection between the original analytical objective and the decisions made throughout the investigation.

articles.title: Learning Python After a Few Years of Go: What Surprised Me So Far
articles.description: I've been writing Go for a few years: explicit types, go mod, goroutines, if err != nil, and the...
articles.body_html:
I've been writing Go for a few years: explicit types, go mod, goroutines, if err != nil, and the comfort of the compiler saying "no" before deploy. Recently I started learning Python.

I'm new to Python, but not new to programming. So this isn't a generic language comparison, and it isn't written by a Python expert. It's what I've actually discovered so far as a Go-heavy brain meeting a dynamic, batteries-included ecosystem.

If you're an experienced Pythonista and I got something wrong, please tell me in the comments. If you're coming from Go too, I hope this saves you a few surprises.

What stayed familiar

Some things translated almost one-to-one.

  • Modules and imports. Files and packages still organize code. You still manage dependencies, just with a virtual environment and pyproject.toml or requirements.txt instead of go.mod.
  • Maps and iteration. Python dicts and for key, value in ... feel like Go maps and range, with less typing and different missing-key behavior (.get() vs (v, ok)).
  • Functions as values. Closures and callbacks exist in both. In Python they show up everywhere (decorators, key= arguments, lambdas) more than in typical Go style.
  • Testing culture. Table-driven tests have a cousin in pytest parametrization. The habit of "many cases, one function" carries over well.

What surprised me

1. Variables aren't typed slots, they're names on objects

In Go, var x int and x := 10 attach a type to a variable. In Python, x = 10 binds a name to an object. Reassigning x = "hello" is legal: the name moved, and the old int may still exist elsewhere.

That one idea explains a lot of "why did it do that?" moments. Assignment doesn't copy a struct-like value by default. It copies a reference, so mutating a list or dict through one name affects every name pointing at that object.

Discovery: I stopped looking for type declarations on every line and started asking: what object does this name point to, and is it mutable?

2. There is no compile-time safety net unless you build one

Go trained me to trust the compiler. Python runs first and complains later.

Type hints (def f(x: int) -> str:) don't change runtime behavior, but running mypy or Pyright in CI gives you a slice of Go-like checking.

Discovery: Professional Python often means type hints + a linter + tests, not "dynamic means anything goes."

3. "No pointers" doesn't mean "no aliasing"

For immutable things (int, str, tuple), behavior often looks like pass-by-value. For lists, dicts, and custom objects, it's shared mutation.

When I need a copy, I have to ask for one (list.copy(), copy.deepcopy()). Go made this obvious with * and &. Python hides it behind semantics.

This leads straight into the first gotcha I ran into.

Gotcha: mutable default arguments 

def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add_item("a"))  # ['a']
print(add_item("b"))  # ['a', 'b']  <- surprise!

The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared across calls. The usual fix:

def add_item(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

Gotcha: == vs is 

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]

print(a == b)  # True  (same value)
print(a is b)  # False (different objects)

Use == to compare values and is to check identity. The main place you want is is x is None.

4. Error handling is a culture shift

My Go reflex:

if err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err)
}

Python's default is exceptions that bubble up until something catches them. Idiomatic code often raises deep inside and catches at boundaries (a CLI command, an HTTP handler, a job runner) rather than around every line.

Discovery: Check explicitly for expected failures like validation and parsing, and use exceptions for exceptional paths or deep call stacks. Both are professional. The mix is the lesson.

5. Cleanup is with, not defer 

with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()

Discovery: Context managers are to Python what defer is to Go: the idiomatic way to say "always release this."

6. Concurrency is a different animal

  • CPU-bound work: the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) limits threads for compute-heavy code, so processes or native extensions matter.
  • I/O-bound work: asyncio (async / await) is the closest mental model to lightweight goroutines, but it's cooperative and depends on async-aware libraries.

Here's the same idea, three tasks running concurrently. First Go:

var wg sync.WaitGroup
results := make([]int, 3)

for i := range results {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        time.Sleep(time.Second)
        results[i] = (i + 1) * 2
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
fmt.Println(results) // [2 4 6]

And Python:

import asyncio

async def work(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return n * 2

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(work(1), work(2), work(3))
    print(results)  # [2, 4, 6]

asyncio.run(main())

The Python version is shorter, but I have to remember that everything in the chain must be async, and one blocking call can stall the whole event loop.

A note on the GIL: recent Python versions include an optional free-threaded build that removes it. Check the current status for the version you use before relying on it.

Discovery: I now map problems to asyncio vs threading vs multiprocessing instead of reaching for goroutines by default.

7. The standard library is huge

JSON, HTTP, pathlib, dataclasses, logging: a lot is already included. I still reach for pytest, httpx or requests, and pydantic where Go might use a few well-known dependencies.

8. dataclass is my struct comfort zone 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int

For API payloads and DTOs, dataclass or Pydantic scratch the same itch as Go structs with JSON tags.

Types and values: a map for Go eyes

Go Python (what I use in practice)
int, float64 int (arbitrary precision), float
string, []byte str, bytes
[]T slice list (mixed types allowed)
map[K]V dict
struct @dataclass or class
interface duck typing, or typing.Protocol for contracts
nil None (use is None, not == None)
zero value no universal zero; know the falsy values (None, 0, "", [], {})
(v, ok) .get(key), or try / except KeyError
  • Numbers: / is true division (5 / 2 gives 2.5), and // is floor division.
  • Strings: f-strings (f"{name}: {score}") replace most day-to-day fmt.Sprintf.
  • Tuples and sets: Go has no first-class versions of these. Python has immutable tuples (1, 2) and sets {1, 2, 3}.
  • Booleans: Python has many falsy values, which is broader than Go's zero-value checks. For optional values, if x is None is not the same as if not x.

Importing code: what Go made obvious, and what Python does differently

In Go, imports are rigid: one module path, one package per directory, exported names capitalized. Python looks simpler (import foo), but the rules live in file layout, packages, and convention.

Mental model: module, package, file

Go Python
Module = repo + go.mod Project = folder with pyproject.toml / requirements.txt
Package = directory with a shared package name Package = directory (often with __init__.py)
File = part of one package Module = one .py file (utils.py is module utils)

Go:

import "github.com/acme/myapp/internal/auth"

auth.Middleware()

Python:

from myapp.auth.middleware import require_token

The layout has to match what Python can find on sys.path, not just what you wish the folder tree looked like.

Import styles 

import json
json.loads('{"a": 1}')

from json import loads
loads('{"a": 1}')

import json as js
from pathlib import Path
  • import module is good for large or clash-prone modules (os, logging).
  • from module import name is idiomatic for small, clear APIs (from dataclasses import dataclass).

Go's closest habit is import aliases (import f "fmt"). Python uses from and aliases constantly, and that's normal.

Where Python looks for modules

  1. The standard library
  2. Packages in the active virtual environment
  3. Your project root, if it's on sys.path (run from the root, pip install -e ., or use PYTHONPATH)

Discovery: Running from the wrong directory, or forgetting the venv, feels like pre-modules Go. Imports fail at runtime. One venv per project is non-optional, just like go.mod per service.

Project layout (mirroring Go instincts) 

src/myapp/
    __init__.py
    main.py
    auth/
        __init__.py
        middleware.py
        service.py
pyproject.toml

Go's internal/ is enforced by the compiler. Python's "private" is a _leading_underscore: convention, not a rule.

Go Python
Foo / foo _helper means "internal, please don't"

Callers can still import _helper. The discipline is social and enforced in code review.

Importing functions, classes, and constants 

# auth/service.py
def validate(token: str) -> bool:
    ...

class User:
    ...

from auth.service import validate, User
# or
from auth import service
service.validate("...")

Packages often re-export a clean surface in __init__.py:

# auth/__init__.py
from .service import validate, User

__all__ = ["validate", "User"]

Relative imports (inside a package only) 

# auth/middleware.py
from .service import validate
from ..config import settings

Go uses full paths only, with no ... Relative imports break if you run a nested file directly (python auth/middleware.py). Prefer python -m myapp or an installed package, similar to running from the module root in Go.

init vs import-time code

Go has func init() at package load. In Python, importing a module runs it once, and __init__.py runs when the package is first imported. I keep __init__.py thin: re-exports and docs, not heavy side effects.

Circular imports

This is the same class of problem as Go import cycles. Fixes: extract a small shared module, import lazily inside a function, or restructure the packages.

Third-party dependencies

Use pip install plus a lockfile (Poetry, uv, and others). Watch for PyPI name vs import name: pip install Pillow gives you import PIL.

Library vs entrypoint 

def main():
    ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Importing the file loads the definitions but does not run main(). It only runs when the file is executed as a script, which is like separating package auth from cmd/server.

Import cheat sheet

I want to... Go Python
Import a package import "path/pkg" import pkg
Use one function pkg.F() from pkg import F
Rename import p "path/pkg" import pkg as p
Hide internals lowercase name _name
Entrypoint func main() in cmd/... if __name__ == "__main__": or python -m pkg
Local monorepo lib replace in go.mod pip install -e ./libs/foo

Functions, control flow, and iteration

Go has multiple returns, defer, and C-style for. Python has a single return value (use tuples for several), with instead of defer, and for x in iterable as the default loop.

Comprehensions are idiomatic where Go would use a loop plus append:

squares = [n * n for n in range(10)]

Variadic functions: Go uses ...T, Python uses *args and **kwargs.

What Go still does better

Learning Python hasn't made me love Go any less. A few things I miss:

  • Compile-time errors. Typos in rarely-run code paths only show up when they run.
  • Single-binary deployment. go build and ship one file. Python needs an environment, dependencies, or a container.
  • Built-in concurrency. Goroutines and channels need no async/await coloring of your functions.
  • Predictable performance for CPU-heavy work.

Neither language is "better." They optimize for different things.

What I'm still figuring out

Being honest, here's what hasn't clicked yet:

  • Async code in larger projects, and how to mix it with blocking libraries
  • Packaging and dependency tools (pip, Poetry, uv): which one, and when
  • When to use a plain class, a dataclass, or a Pydantic model
  • Reading and writing good type hints for more complex code

If you have advice on any of these, I'd really like to hear it.

Habits I deliberately changed

  1. A virtualenv for every project, like a non-optional go.mod.
  2. Type-hint public APIs, and let tools enforce them.
  3. Use with, comprehensions, and pytest, instead of translating every Go loop.
  4. Catch exceptions at the edges rather than copying if err != nil onto every line.
  5. Treat is None and falsiness as different checks.
  6. Use an editable install (pip install -e .) so from myapp... imports behave like a real module graph.

Closing

Learning Python as a Go developer isn't a downgrade or a "scripting detour." It's a language optimized for expression speed and ecosystem breadth, where discipline shows up in tests, types, project layout, and imports as much as in the compiler.

The uncomfortable parts (dynamic typing, exceptions, the GIL, import paths) aren't gaps in my education. They're different tradeoffs. Once I named them (references vs values, boundaries vs inline errors, asyncio vs goroutines, modules vs go.mod), Python stopped feeling like "Go with missing braces" and started feeling like a tool I'm getting comfortable with.

If you're coming from Go too, you're not starting from zero. You're retargeting a structured mindset.

Your turn: What surprised you most when you switched languages? Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: Type a pipe() That Checks Every Step: Variadic Tuples, infer and One Recursive Type
articles.description: Effect types pipe() with 20 overloads. Build one recursive type that checks every step, test it with @ts-expect-error, and see where overloads still win.
articles.body_html:
• Book: The TypeScript Type System
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Open Effect's Function.ts and count the signatures of pipe. There are 20: one for a bare value, then one more for every extra function, up to 19. RxJS 7's standalone pipe types nine functions and then falls back to a catch-all signature that returns UnaryFunction<T, unknown>. Hand it a tenth function and the output type is gone.

Those libraries know exactly what they are doing. When TypeScript 4.0 shipped variadic tuple types, the release notes called this pattern "death by a thousand overloads", and overloads are still how the big libraries type pipe. The reason is that a single generic signature that checks every step is harder to write than it looks, and it gives some things up.

You're going to write that single signature anyway: about 40 lines of types, checked by tsc --noEmit, and then the four places it breaks so you know when overloads win.

Step 1: read the ends with infer

Start with four small helpers. In and Out pull the parameter and return type out of a one-argument function. First and Last pull the first and last element out of a tuple.

// pipe.ts
export type Fn = (arg: any) => any;

type In<F> = F extends (arg: infer A) => any ? A : never;
type Out<F> = F extends (arg: any) => infer R ? R : never;

type First<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer F, ...unknown[]] ? F : never;
type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...unknown[], infer L] ? L : never;

Last matches with a leading rest element, [...unknown[], infer L], which TypeScript has accepted since 4.2. With these you can write the obvious pipe type: the input of the first function, the output of the last.

type NaivePipe<Fns extends Fn[]> =
  (input: In<First<Fns>>) => Out<Last<Fns>>;

It reads the ends and never looks at the middle. Give it trim (string to string), len (string to number) and shout (string to string) and it reports (input: string) => string, even though shout would receive a number at runtime. A pipe type that only reads the ends is an as cast with better marketing.


Reading only the first input and the last output leaves every joint in the middle unchecked.

Step 2: walk the list with one recursive type

The real check has to visit every adjacent pair. Recursive conditional types (TypeScript 4.1) let a type refer to itself in its own branches, so you peel one function off the front, compare its input with the value flowing in, and recurse on the rest.

type PipeError<Step, Got, Want> = {
  readonly error: "pipe(): a step got the wrong input";
  readonly step: Step;
  readonly got: Got;
  readonly want: Want;
};

type Check<
  Fns extends Fn[],
  Input,
  Cur,
  Done extends unknown[] = []
> = Fns extends [infer F, ...infer Rest extends Fn[]]
  ? [Cur] extends [In<F>]
    ? Check<Rest, Input, Out<F>, [...Done, F]>
    : PipeError<[...Done, F]["length"], Cur, In<F>>
  : (input: Input) => Cur;

export type Pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]> = Check<
  Fns,
  In<First<Fns>>,
  In<First<Fns>>
>;

Four details carry the weight here.

infer Rest extends Fn[] puts a constraint on the inferred rest, a feature from TypeScript 4.7. Without it, Rest can't be passed back into Check, whose first parameter demands Fn[].

[Cur] extends [In<F>] wraps both sides in brackets on purpose. A bare Cur extends ... on a type parameter is distributive: if a step returns string | number, the check would split into one branch per member and hand you a union of a function and an error. The brackets compare the whole union at once.

Done collects the functions already visited. Its only job is to number the failing step: [...Done, F]["length"] is the 1-based position of F as a number literal type.

The recursive call is the entire branch result. Nothing wraps it, and that makes Check tail-recursive, which matters when chains get long.

The runtime part is short:

export function pipe<Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]]>(
  ...fns: Fns
): Pipe<Fns> {
  const run = (input: unknown) =>
    fns.reduce((acc: unknown, fn) => fn(acc), input);
  return run as unknown as Pipe<Fns>;
}

Fns extends [Fn, ...Fn[]] on a rest parameter makes TypeScript infer the arguments as a tuple, one element per function, which is what Check walks. The double cast is the honest part: the body can't prove a deferred conditional type, so you assert once at the boundary and callers get the checked type. The overloaded libraries pay the same toll in their own way; Effect's implementation signature is pipe(a: unknown, ...args: Array<any>): unknown.

Step 3: prove it with @ts-expect-error

A type you can't test is a type you will break by accident. // @ts-expect-error (TypeScript 3.9) suppresses the error on the next line, and if that line has no error, tsc reports Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive. That turns every expected failure into an assertion.

// pipe.types.ts
import { pipe } from "./pipe";

type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends
  (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)
    ? true
    : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

const trim = (s: string) => s.trim();
const len = (s: string) => s.length;
const isLong = (n: number) => n > 10;
const shout = (s: string) => s.toUpperCase();

const ok = pipe(trim, len, isLong);
export type OkIsTyped = Expect<
  Equal<typeof ok, (input: string) => boolean>
>;

// @ts-expect-error the input must be a string
ok(42);

const broken = pipe(trim, len, shout);

// @ts-expect-error step 3 wants a string, gets a number
broken("  hello  ");

// @ts-expect-error a broken pipe is not a function
const f: (s: string) => string = broken;

// @ts-expect-error pipe() needs at least one step
pipe();

Equal compares two types strictly, so a result that drifts to any or to a wider type fails it; Expect fails to compile when handed false. A minimal tsconfig.json next to the two files:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler"
  },
  "include": ["pipe.ts", "pipe.types.ts"]
}

Install the compiler with npm i -D typescript, then run npx tsc. The config needs TypeScript 5.0 or newer for "moduleResolution": "bundler"; the types themselves need 4.7. If any expectation stops holding, either an Expect line or an unused directive fails the build, locally or in CI.

Where the recursive version breaks

Look again at the broken test. The pipe(trim, len, shout) line compiles. The type of broken is PipeError<3, number, string>, and the error only appears where you call it or assign it to a function type. Hovering broken tells you the step, what it got and what it wanted, which beats a silent unknown, but the red squiggle sits on the wrong line. Overloads don't have this problem: each step is its own parameter, so a mismatch is an argument error on the exact function that's wrong. There is a variant that rewrites the rest parameter to the expected tuple so the error moves onto the bad argument; ecyrbe's write-up shows one. I haven't run it, and a commenter there reports a gap in its first-to-second step check, so test it the same way before you trust it.

Generic steps lose their type parameter. Take const wrap = <T>(x: T): T[] => [x]. When In and Out match a generic signature against infer, the type parameter doesn't survive; TypeScript issue #38964 shows ReturnType of <T = string>() => T coming out as unknown. So pipe(trim, wrap, join), with join taking string[], fails with got: unknown[]. The fix is an instantiation expression (4.7): pass wrap<string> as the step and the chain checks. Overloads get this for free, because each step is matched against (a: A) => B with A already known, and since TypeScript 3.4 a composer can even propagate a generic step's type parameters into the result.

Inline lambdas aren't typed from the previous step. In Effect, pipe(" hi ", (s) => s.trim(), (s) => s.length) types each s from the step before it, because every overload names the intermediate types as separate type parameters. In ...fns: Fns, nothing ties the second slot's parameter to the first slot's return, so an unannotated (s) => s.length has no way to learn that s is a string. The best it gets is the any from the Fn constraint, and an any step checks nothing. Annotate every inline step, or write the steps as named functions.

Long chains hit the depth limit, depending on how you wrote the recursion. The TypeScript PR that added tail-recursion elimination lets tail-recursive conditional types loop 1,000 times before giving up, and lowered the general limit for the rest to 100. Check is tail-recursive, so a 30-step pipe is nowhere near the ceiling. Rewrite it so the recursive call sits inside something else, a tuple spread or a union, and you are back under the general limit, where the failure is the familiar Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite from the 4.5 release notes. Even well under the limit, the 4.1 notes warn that recursive types can increase type-checking time, so keep the step types themselves simple.

When overloads are still the better choice


Overloads write one signature per chain length. The recursive type writes one signature that walks the list.

The rule that falls out of the four breaks: choose by who writes the steps.

If callers write steps inline, as lambdas, or pass generic helpers like map and filter, use overloads. That is the RxJS and Effect situation, where most steps are operators with type parameters and most callbacks are unannotated. Contextual typing per step and per-argument errors are worth more than an unlimited chain length, and very few real pipelines need more than the 19 functions Effect covers.

If callers pass named, already-typed, non-generic functions, use the recursive type. Validation chains, middleware lists and data transforms assembled from a registry all fit: the steps already carry their own types, chains can be longer than any overload stack, and the PipeError type names the failing step. Ship it with the @ts-expect-error file so the next refactor can't quietly break the check.

If this was useful

The recursive Check type is a small version of a pattern that keeps coming back: walk a tuple with infer, carry state in an accumulator, keep the recursion in tail position. The TypeScript Type System goes deep on that toolkit: generics, mapped and conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types. If you already write TypeScript daily, that's the one to read next; if you're still getting comfortable with narrowing and modules, start with TypeScript Essentials.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Coming from Kotlin, Java or PHP? The two bridge books replace the first two for you. Shipping TypeScript at work, with build tooling and published packages? TypeScript in Production covers that layer.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.description: Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 1  I do this thing sometimes where I get an idea at the wrong time. Not...
articles.body_html:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 1

I do this thing sometimes where I get an idea at the wrong time. Not when I have free hours and a clear head, but at 1 AM, mid-week, while I should be doing something else entirely. The idea lands and refuses to leave.

The idea this time was simple on the surface: what if I built a database?

Not a production database. Not the next MongoDB or a distributed cloud thing. Just a small, honest, embedded database. One file, one process, document storage. Something I could actually finish understanding from top to bottom, because I was starting to realize that I had been using databases for years without really knowing what they were doing inside.

That bothered me.

So I started nosqlite. An experiment. A learning project. And what you are reading now is me trying to document how I built it, what I learned, and what it taught me about databases, data structures, systems programming, and Rust itself.

What Are We Actually Building

The description in the README is honest: "trying to build a small embedded nosql database from scratch in rust."

The name is a mashup of two real things: NoSQL and SQLite. Not because it is trying to replace either, but because it takes inspiration from both.

SQLite is one of the most deployed software libraries in human history. Every Android phone has it. Every iOS app probably uses it. Browsers use it. It is a self-contained database that lives in a single file. You do not start a server. You just open a file and start reading and writing. That simplicity is profound when you think about it. The whole database is just a file you can cp, mv, or put on a USB drive.

NoSQL is a broader idea. It basically means "not relational." Instead of tables with fixed columns, you store documents. A document is just a blob of structured data, something like JSON. The shape can vary per record. You do not declare a schema upfront. This model made a lot of sense for applications where data is fluid and hard to predict.

nosqlite tries to marry these two ideas. SQLite-like single file simplicity. NoSQL-like document storage.

That is the goal. And it is entirely an experiment.

Why I Built This in Rust

I was already shifting toward Rust as my primary language. I wrote about that decision separately. But this project cemented it.

Rust is the right tool for something like this because a database engine is fundamentally a systems problem. You are dealing with raw bytes. You are managing a file at the byte level. You are thinking about memory layout, about what happens when a process crashes mid-write, about how data is read back and verified. These are not higher-level concerns.

In TypeScript or Python, you would reach for a library to handle most of this. In Rust, you can actually go down to the level of reading four bytes at a known offset and interpreting them as a little-endian u32. You can describe the exact memory layout of a page. You can write a function that writes bytes into a buffer at a cursor position and have the type system enforce that you do not mess it up.

And the borrow checker, which every newcomer to Rust finds frustrating, becomes genuinely valuable when you are building something like this. You cannot accidentally have two mutable references to the same page buffer. The compiler forces you to think about ownership at every step, which turns out to be exactly what you want when you are building a storage engine.

Understanding What a Database Actually Is

Most developers, including me before this project, have a mental model of a database that looks something like: "you write a query, rows come back." That is the interface. The internals stay hidden.

Here is the simpler version of what actually happens.

A database is ultimately a program that manages a file. The file is structured in a very specific way so that the database can find things quickly, can guarantee that data is not corrupted, and can handle the program crashing at any moment without losing committed data.

Every database, whether it is SQLite or PostgreSQL, has roughly the same set of problems to solve:

How do you organize bytes in the file? You cannot just write raw data one record after another and hope for the best. You need structure. Databases use the concept of a page. A page is a fixed-size chunk of the file, usually 4096 bytes, which matches the OS's memory page size. The database reads and writes entire pages at once.

How do you find records? If every lookup required scanning the entire file, a database with millions of records would be unusably slow. This is where data structures like B-trees come in. B-trees let you find records in logarithmic time. nosqlite does not have a full B-tree index yet, but it is on the roadmap, and I will cover it in a later article.

How do you handle crashes? If you are in the middle of writing when the power goes out, your data should not become corrupt garbage. Most databases solve this with write-ahead logging, abbreviated WAL. You write your intention to a log first, then perform the actual write. On startup, you replay the log. nosqlite plans to implement WAL, but this is also future territory.

How do you support multiple users accessing the same database? This is the concurrency problem. nosqlite currently takes the simple path: only one process can open the database at a time, enforced with a lock file.

The Structure of nosqlite

The project is a Rust workspace with three crates:

nosqlite-core is the storage engine. Everything that reads from and writes to the database file lives here. The pager, the page layout, the catalog (which tracks collections), the document storage logic, the binary codec.

nosqlite-ffi is a C ABI bindings layer. It exposes the core engine through a C-compatible API so that other languages can use it. Go and Python bindings already exist. Dart/Flutter bindings are planned.

nosqlite-shell is a command-line shell. You can open a database file, create collections, insert documents, query them, and delete them, all from the terminal.

That layered design matters. The core does not know or care about what calls it. The FFI layer wraps it in a way that any language with a C FFI can use. The shell is just one consumer among many.

NoSQL Concepts You Need to Know

Before the next articles get into code, it is worth establishing the vocabulary.

Database is the top-level container. In nosqlite, it maps to a single file.

Collection is roughly equivalent to a table in a relational database, but without a fixed schema. In MongoDB, you would call this a collection. In nosqlite, that is the term too.

Document is a single record within a collection. A document is a structured blob of data. nosqlite stores documents in BSON format, which stands for Binary JSON. BSON is what MongoDB uses under the hood. It is like JSON but binary-encoded, which makes it faster to parse and more efficient to store.

ObjectId is a unique identifier automatically assigned to every document. It is a 12-byte value that encodes a timestamp, a machine identifier, and a counter. This is also borrowed from MongoDB.

A typical interaction with nosqlite looks like this through its shell:

create users
insert users { "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
find users
[
{ "_id": "...", "name": "Priyanshu", "age": 22 }
]

Simple. Intentionally simple. The focus is on understanding what happens under the hood when you type those commands.

The Experiment Mindset

I want to be honest about something. This project is not finished. It probably will not be "finished" in a traditional sense. I am building it as I learn, which means some commits introduce bugs, some commits fix them, and some commits just rename things because I changed my mind about the design. All of that is in the public history.

I am okay with that. This is not a portfolio piece trying to impress someone. It is a record of me figuring things out in public. I find that approach more useful than studying theory alone. When something breaks and I have to debug it at the byte level, I actually understand it. Reading about it in a book does not give me the same thing.

Each article in this series follows the same pattern: a feature lands, I write about it. What the problem was, what I built, what it taught me, what I am still not sure about.

The repository is at https://github.com/PriyanshuPz/nosqlite . The commit history is open. You can see exactly what changed and when.

Now here is the thing that kept me up when I started this project. I had a blank file. A completely empty .nsql file on disk. And I had to decide: what does byte zero mean? What is the very first thing I write? What does the engine look for when it opens that file tomorrow and needs to trust that it is valid?

That question sounds simple. It is not. And the answer to it is the entire next article.

articles.title: Inferred Type Predicates Won't Save filter(Boolean). Here's What Will.
articles.description: TypeScript 5.5 added inferred type predicates, and the internet decided that meant filter(Boolean) finally narrows. It doesn't. Here's exactly what the feature fixed, why the mix-up happened, and the one-line pattern that actually gets you type-safe filtering.
articles.body_html:
Open any "what's new in TypeScript 5.5" roundup from the last two years and you'll find some version of the same line: inferred type predicates finally fixed .filter(Boolean). It gets repeated because it's satisfying — a years-old annoyance, solved for free, no code changes needed. It also isn't true.

The feature that's actually in 5.5 is narrower than the myth, and more useful once you see what it's really for. You've probably been deleting type guards you didn't need to delete, right next to a .filter(Boolean) that's just as untyped as it was in 2019.

The claim, and why it's believable

Here's the example every one of those roundups leads with. Before TypeScript 5.5, this didn't narrow:

const maybeNumbers = [1, null, 2, null, 3];

// previously: (number | null)[] — TypeScript didn't trust the callback
const numbers = maybeNumbers.filter((n) => n !== null);

You wrote a callback that obviously removes null, ran it, and TypeScript still handed you back (number | null)[]. The only way to get a real number[] was to spell it out by hand:

const numbers = maybeNumbers.filter(
  (n): n is number => n !== null
);

That (n): n is number => syntax is a type predicate — a little promise to the compiler that says "if this returns true, treat the input as this narrower type." Writing it by hand, every time, for a check this obvious, was the exact kind of busywork TypeScript is supposed to save you from. TypeScript 5.5 fixed it: the plain (n) => n !== null now gets the predicate inferred automatically. No annotation. Same code, better type.

So far, every word of the popular claim checks out. Here's where it quietly goes off the rails.

Try the one line everyone actually writes

Nobody filters nulls with n !== null in real code nearly as often as they reach for the shorthand:

const configs = [getConfig(), null, getConfig(), undefined];

// still (Config | null | undefined)[] in every TypeScript version as of this writing
const valid = configs.filter(Boolean);

Paste that into the TypeScript playground. The result is still (Config | null | undefined)[] — the exact array you started with, falsy values and all. The feature that rewrote n !== null into a type guard does nothing here, on the single most common one-liner for exactly this job.

Quick gut check before you scroll: what's different between (n) => n !== null and Boolean, if they do the same job?

Why the compiler can see one and not the other

Inferred type predicates work by TypeScript reading a function's body and recognizing a pattern: one return statement, no implicit fall-through, the parameter isn't reassigned, and the thing being returned is a boolean check tied directly to that parameter. (n) => n !== null qualifies on every count — it's a tiny, transparent function, and the compiler can see exactly what it decides and why.

Boolean isn't a function you wrote. It's the global constructor, declared in TypeScript's own standard library as a call signature with no visible implementation — (value?: any) => boolean, full stop. There's no body for the inference engine to read, because as far as the type checker is concerned, there's no body at all. It's an ambient declaration, same category as parseInt or Array.isArray: TypeScript trusts the signature you gave it and nothing more. Teaching the compiler to special-case .filter(Boolean) specifically would mean hard-coding one function name into the type checker — not inference, a workaround with a name attached.

That's the actual boundary of the 5.5 feature: it infers predicates from code it can read. Boolean was never going to be included, in 5.5 or any release after it, unless the standard library itself grows a dedicated overload for it — which, as of this writing, it hasn't.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Why the mix-up happened

Nobody misreported this out of carelessness. .filter(n => n !== null) and .filter(Boolean) solve the identical problem and read, to a human, like two spellings of the same idea. The release notes' headline example uses the first form because it's the clean one to explain in a changelog. Readers who've spent years typing the second form saw "filter now narrows" and reasonably assumed their own habit was covered.

It's the kind of gap that only shows up when you actually run the code, which most roundups — understandably, on a deadline — don't.

What to actually do with your type guards

The real payoff of 5.5 is that you can delete annotations you were writing by hand, as long as the function itself is one TypeScript can read:

// before 5.5 — had to spell out the predicate yourself
function isDefined<T>(value: T): value is NonNullable<T> {
  return value != null;
}

// 5.5+ — this now infers the exact same predicate, with no `is` anywhere
function isDefined<T>(value: T) {
  return value != null;
}

const valid = configs.filter(isDefined); // Config[] — for real this time

That's a genuine win: a helper function you've probably had in a utils.ts file for years just got shorter, and any arrow function shaped like it gets the same treatment for free. What it isn't is a reason to rip out isDefined and go back to .filter(Boolean) for brevity — that one line is exactly where the narrowing still doesn't reach. If you want the one-liner and the types, write the predicate yourself:

const valid = configs.filter(
  (c): c is NonNullable<typeof c> => Boolean(c)
);

Same runtime behavior as .filter(Boolean), three extra words, and an array type you can actually trust downstream.

The takeaway

TypeScript 5.5 didn't make filter(Boolean) type-safe — it made your own boolean-returning functions smart enough that you stop writing is annotations for them by hand. Keep the named helper, drop its predicate syntax, and reach for the explicit inline predicate only when you actually want the Boolean-style one-liner. The compiler was never going to read minds; it just got better at reading your functions.

Next time a changelog claims a one-line fix for a years-old annoyance, paste the actual snippet into the playground before you repeat it. What's one you've seen repeated that didn't hold up?
