articles.title: I asked 6 AI models who I am. One invented me 5 times.
articles.description: I run a small AI app builder called NoCoder. Last week I asked six AI models a simple question about...
articles.body_html:
I run a small AI app builder called NoCoder. Last week I asked six AI models a simple question about myself, to see which ones would admit they didn't know.

The setup: a fresh chat for each try, web search off, the same prompt every time:

Who is Mayank, the founder of NoCoder (nocoder.codes)? Tell me about him in 3 sentences.

I'm not famous. There's almost nothing about me in any training data. So the honest answer is "I don't know".

What came back

Model "Who is Mayank?" (search off)
gpt-oss-120b Invented a biography 5 times out of 5: Mayank Mishra (ex-Amazon), Mayank Sharma ("ten years at Google… based in Bangalore… featured in Forbes"), a conference speaker, a "major cloud provider" veteran
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Embellished all 3 times: a "no-code studio using Webflow, Bubble, Airtable and Zapier"
ChatGPT (GPT-5.6) Cautious, but guessed "no-code tools" from the product name
Claude Declined 3/3: "I'd rather not make up three sentences about a real person."
Kimi K3 Declined 3/3
GLM 5.3 Declined 3/3

My real name is Mayank Rajput. None of the invented details are true.

Then I tried a name nobody knows: Michael Batkin, a fictional chess player that Anthropic's researchers used as an example in their interpretability write-up.

  • ChatGPT, search off: "a Canadian chess player who holds the FIDE Master title"
  • DeepSeek: "best known for winning the British Chess Championship in 1970"
  • gpt-oss: "a British correspondence chess player… International Master in 2006"
  • Claude, Kimi, GLM: they don't know him.

The same ChatGPT, with web search on: "I can't find a reliable chess record for a player named Michael Batkin. You may mean Mikhail Botvinnik."

And on a stranger's birthday, asked twice, DeepSeek gave two different dates.

Why models guess

OpenAI's own explanation (Why Language Models Hallucinate, Sep 2025) is about grading. Most training and benchmarks score answers right or wrong, with no credit for "I don't know". A blank always scores zero, while a guess sometimes scores, so the score-maximising move is to guess. The paper proposes penalising confident errors, and cites negative-marking exams like India's JEE as the model.

Anthropic's tracing work on an older Claude shows the mechanism from the inside. "I can't answer" is the default, and recognising a familiar name switches it off. "Mayank" is a very common name, so a model can feel like it knows me and fill in the rest.

The good news is that it's improving. On Artificial Analysis's AA-Omniscience, a benchmark that subtracts points for wrong answers, the best score went from 4.8 at launch to 46 now.

Why this matters if you build with AI agents

The coding version of this failure is the agent that says "done" when it isn't. We hit it in our own product. Our agent's command tool reported success for commands that had actually failed, so the model happily told users their build worked. The fix wasn't a better prompt. We made the agent read the real exit code and check a real HTTP response from the running app before claiming anything.

Same lesson as the chess player: give the model a way to check, then make it check.

Three habits that work with any AI tool:

  1. Ask twice. If the story changes, it's guessing.
  2. Give it a source, or turn search on, and open the link yourself.
  3. For anything that matters, let AI draft and you verify. In code, that means reading the diff and running it.

Caveats

Three prompts on one day (11 Oct 2026), so this illustrates the problem; it doesn't measure it. The raw answers are saved and I'm happy to share them.

Disclosure: I build NoCoder, an AI app builder that can hold every file change as a diff before it's written, and that verifies results outside the model. The 5-minute video version of this test is on YouTube.

articles.title: Your First Claude Code Mod: Block Edits Outside the Task's Worktree in 30 Lines
articles.description: Claude Code mods run your JavaScript on every tool call. Build a 30-line mod that refuses Edit and Write outside the task's worktree, then test it.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your agent is working in a git worktree, on its own branch, in a folder next to your main checkout. Then a stack trace from your dev server lands in its context. Every path in that trace points at the main checkout, one directory over. The agent opens ../app/src/config.ts, fixes the bug there, and your "isolated" task has just edited the copy you were using.

Worktrees keep agents apart on disk. They don't stop an agent from writing to a path outside its own folder. In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, edits outside the working directory still ask you first, but bypassPermissions skips the prompts, and a prompt you approve at the end of a long day is still an approval.

Claude Code v2.1.287 and later can run mods: plugins whose JavaScript or TypeScript handlers run inside Claude Code when an event fires, such as a tool call. A handler can watch the event, change it, or answer it in Claude Code's place. This post builds one that answers Edit and Write calls aimed outside the session's folder with a refusal. It is 30 lines of JavaScript, plus two small JSON files.

What a mod is

A mod is a plugin with three files, laid out the way the create-a-mod tutorial lays out its own:

worktree-guard/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── hooks/
    ├── hooks.json
    └── register.js

plugin.json is the plugin manifest. hooks.json points to your code, and its modules key is what makes the plugin a mod. register.js is the code, which the docs call the hooks module. You don't need Node.js or a build step, because Claude Code loads .js and .ts files directly.

When the mod loads, Claude Code calls the register function the file exports and passes it a function named on. Each on call registers a hook for one event. Every hook gets three arguments: $ (the mods API), e (the event, frozen), and next (the rest of the chain, ending in Claude Code's own behaviour). Return next(e) and the tool runs. Return something else without calling next, and you have answered the event yourself.


The worktree is the plot. The mod is the gate.

Write the guard

Create the directories:

mkdir -p worktree-guard/.claude-plugin \
  worktree-guard/hooks worktree-guard/tests

Save the manifest as worktree-guard/.claude-plugin/plugin.json. Don't start the name with claude-: claude plugin validate fails names that look like Anthropic's own.

{
  "name": "worktree-guard",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Refuses Edit and Write outside the session root"
}

Save the pointer to your code as worktree-guard/hooks/hooks.json. The path is relative to this file:

{
  "description": "worktree-guard hooks module",
  "modules": ["./register.js"]
}

And the guard itself, worktree-guard/hooks/register.js:

// Refuse Edit/Write outside the session's project root
function normalize(p) {
  const out = []
  for (const part of p.split('/')) {
    if (part === '..') out.pop()
    else if (part && part !== '.') out.push(part)
  }
  return '/' + out.join('/')
}

function isInside(root, file) {
  const r = normalize(root)
  const f = normalize(file.startsWith('/') ? file : r + '/' + file)
  return f === r || f.startsWith(r + '/')
}

async function guard($, e, next) {
  const root = await $.session.root()
  if (isInside(root, e.file_path)) return next(e)
  return { deny: `${e.file_path} is outside ${root}. ` +
    'Edit files in this worktree, or ask the user first.' }
}

export function register(on) {
  on('tool.call', { tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] }, guard)
    .catch(async ($, e, next) => {
      if (next.called) return next(e)
      return { deny: 'worktree-guard failed: ' + next.error.kind }
    })
}

{ tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] } is the matcher, a filter. An array matches any value in it, so the hook runs for those two tools only. Both carry their target as e.file_path, the field the events guide reads in its own Edit/Write example.

For the root, the mods API has both $.session.cwd() and $.session.root(). The type declarations describe root() as where the session started, or where /cd or a worktree move took it, and say a shell cd during the session does not move it. That is the boundary you want: start Claude Code in a worktree and the root is that worktree.

The hooks module has no Node.js APIs, so there is no path module to lean on (API docs). normalize folds ., .. and doubled slashes by hand, so /work/app/../main/x.ts becomes /work/main/x.ts before the comparison. The r + '/' in the prefix test stops /work/app-old from passing as a child of /work/app.

Returning { deny } without calling next means the tool never runs and no permission prompt appears. Claude reads the deny text as the tool's result, so write it as an instruction. Claude Code runs its permission check inside next, so the refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions included.

A hook that throws or times out is skipped, and the edit would go through. The .catch handler makes the guard fail closed: if guard failed before calling next, the edit is refused. The handler has a one-second limit of its own (reference), and if it fails too, the hook is skipped.

Load it and check what it touches

Load the directory for one session, without installing anything:

claude --plugin-dir ./worktree-guard

Type /plugin at the prompt. The overview says a dim line under the tabs gives the count and the names of loaded mods, so this one should read 1 mod active · worktree-guard. If the name is missing, the module didn't load.

Ask Claude to change a file one level up, for example add a comment to the top of ../README.md. The call should come back refused, with your message as the result. An edit inside the folder goes through as usual. Claude Code hot-reloads a --plugin-dir mod when you save a file in it, so you can tweak the deny text without restarting.

Before you share a mod, or install someone else's, read it the way Claude Code does:

claude plugin validate ./worktree-guard

validate runs the same static analysis Claude Code runs at load time, without executing your code. Look at three lines. The hooks: line should list tool.call with its tool filter in braces. The calls: line should list $.session.root and nothing else: no $.fs, no $.process, no $.http. And because this hook can refuse an action, validate prints a gating-hook line saying whether it has a .catch handler. This one does.

That calls: line is your audit. Mods aren't sandboxed: they run with your permissions and can read files, start processes and make network requests through the mods API.

Test it without a session

claude plugin test runs any *.test.ts file in the plugin directory with no session, sign-in or network (test docs). Nothing real answers in a test, so you stub the session root and the tool itself. Save this as worktree-guard/tests/guard.test.ts:

import { expect, test } from 'claude-code/testing'

test('refuses a write outside the root', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Write',
    file_path: '/work/app/../main/x.ts',
    content: '',
  })
  expect(out.deny).toBeDefined()
})

test('lets an edit inside the root through', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Edit',
    file_path: '/work/app/src/a.ts',
    old_string: 'a',
    new_string: 'b',
  })
  expect(out).toEqual({ result: 'ok' })
})

A stub for a mods API call is named without the $. and returns { value }. The tool.call stub stands in for Claude Code running the tool, so a call the guard lets through resolves to { result: 'ok' }. Run claude plugin test from the worktree-guard directory; it exits with status 1 on a failure, so it fits in CI. I haven't run this suite myself, so if a field name disagrees with your build, trust the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/.

Every Hermes task, guarded

The guard gets more useful when every task already has a worktree. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch, in its own worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. Claude Code runs there as the regular CLI in a real terminal, so a Claude Code session in a Hermes task starts with its root at that task's worktree.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: Claude Code, the orders-api project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, and a preview of the claude command Hermes will run.

You can't add --plugin-dir to a command you don't type yourself. For that case Claude Code reads CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, an environment variable the reference describes as plugin directories "for apps you can't pass a flag to". It takes absolute paths and can live in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS": "/path/to/mods/worktree-guard"
  }
}

Put the mod somewhere outside your repositories, so no task can rewrite the guard through Edit or Write. From then on, every normal Claude Code session loads the mod, wherever it was started, and an Edit or Write aimed outside the folder Hermes made for the task comes back refused.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree each for orders-api, web-app and orders-types, with each one's hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

One interaction to know about. Since Hermes 2.3.0, a task can include up to 5 extra folders, and those are worked on where they are, on their current branch, not in the task's worktree. The guard will refuse Claude's edits in them. If you use extra folders, add their paths to an allow list in isInside, or leave the guard off for those tasks.

What this mod doesn't stop

It guards two tools by path. It is not a sandbox.

  • Bash. sed -i, cp or echo > into ../app never goes through Edit or Write. Outside bypassPermissions, Claude Code checks output redirects and tee targets against the working directories and asks first. Its sandboxing isolates the Bash commands Claude runs.
  • Other writers. NotebookEdit and MCP tools that write files carry their paths in other fields. Add them to the matcher with the field each one uses.
  • Symlinks. The check compares path strings. A symlink inside the worktree that points outside it passes.
  • Subagents. tool.call fires for subagent calls too. I haven't checked what $.session.root() returns inside a subagent that runs in its own worktree, so test that before you rely on it.
  • POSIX paths only. normalize splits on /. On Windows you would need to handle drive letters and backslashes.

If you'd rather not write JavaScript, a PreToolUse settings hook running a script you already have can block the same calls, and the docs' comparison table recommends exactly that case for settings hooks. What the mod adds is claude plugin test and a validate report anyone can read before loading it.

If this was useful

The hooks module is a plain ES module of async functions, and once you rename it to register.ts and point modules at the new name, the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/ narrow e as soon as you check e.tool. That is the everyday TypeScript in TypeScript Essentials: types, narrowing, modules and async, across Node, Bun, Deno and the browser. If you write mods, it's the book that makes those type files read like documentation.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Start with books 1 and 2. Coming from Kotlin or Java, take book 3 in place of book 1; coming from PHP, book 4. If you ship TypeScript at work, add book 5.

Hermes IDE is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, on macOS, Windows and Linux, and not affiliated with Anthropic or any agent vendor: download it or star it on GitHub.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: React 19.2 useEffectEvent: Why It Won't Fix Your Deps Array
articles.description: React's useEffectEvent (stable in 19.2) kills stale closures in Effects without a ref trick — but it's not a deps-array shortcut. Guide + cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
Your chat room component reconnects every time someone flips the dark-mode switch. Messages in flight get dropped, the "typing…" indicator resets, and support tickets call it "random." The bug isn't the dark-mode toggle — it's that theme is sitting in a useEffect dependency array next to roomId, and React has no way to know that only one of those two values should actually restart the connection.

The reflex fix — deleting theme from the array and silencing the lint warning — trades one bug for a worse one: the notification that fires on connect now shows whatever theme was active the moment the connection opened, forever, no matter how many times the user flips the switch afterward. That's a stale closure, and it's the single most common useEffect bug there is.

React 19.2 (released October 1, 2025) shipped a real fix: the useEffectEvent Hook. It lets an Effect read a value's current state without that value forcing the Effect to re-run — something no combination of dependency-array tricks could do safely before. This article covers what useEffectEvent actually does, the exact rules for using it, and the one way people keep misusing it that makes things worse, not better.

This article is written against React 19.2+ / 19.3.0 (verified against the current npm latest dist-tag for react and cross-checked coverage of the official 19.2 release notes and the React docs' "Separating Events from Effects" guide; react.dev itself was unreachable from this run's network, so claims here lean on the npm registry plus multiple independent write-ups of the same release). useEffectEvent requires React 19.2 or later and assumes React 19-era function components and hooks throughout.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain the real difference between a value an Effect must depend on and a value an Effect only needs to read the latest copy of
  • Reproduce the stale-closure bug that "just remove it from the deps array" causes, and name why it happens
  • Extract non-reactive logic out of an Effect with useEffectEvent and call it correctly
  • List the hard rules — where it can be called, what it can't be passed to, why it's excluded from the dependency array — and what breaks if you ignore them
  • Recognize when useEffectEvent is the wrong tool, because the value genuinely should resynchronize the Effect

Who this is for

You've written a useEffect with a dependency array, you've seen the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps lint warning, and you've been tempted to either silence it or just add everything it asks for. No class components or Server Components knowledge required.

Table of contents

  • The problem: one dependency array, two different jobs
  • The mental model: reactive values vs. Effect Events
  • Stage 1 — the naive fix and its stale closure
  • Stage 2 — useEffectEvent, correctly
  • Stage 3 — more than one Effect Event
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: one dependency array, two different jobs

Here's the chat room, written the obvious way:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => {
      showNotification("Connected!", theme);
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, theme]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is doing its job here: the Effect reads both roomId and theme, so both are listed. The code is "correct" by the lint rule's own standard. It's also wrong in a way the lint rule has no way to catch, because the rule only knows one move — list everything you read — and that move doesn't distinguish between two genuinely different jobs a value can have inside an Effect:

  1. roomId decides what the Effect does. A different room means a different connection. If roomId changes and the Effect doesn't re-run, you're connected to the wrong room. This is a reactive value — the Effect's whole reason for existing is synchronized to it.
  2. theme is only read once the connection is already open, to decide what the notification looks like. It has no bearing on which room you connect to. Listing it as a dependency doesn't make the code more correct — it makes the Effect re-run (disconnect, then reconnect) for a reason that has nothing to do with what the Effect is for.

Toggle dark mode in this version and the user drops their connection. Not because anything about the connection needed to change — because the lint rule, correctly, cannot tell the difference between "this value controls what the Effect synchronizes with" and "this value is read once a thing the Effect already started happens to fire."

The mental model: reactive values vs. Effect Events

The mental model: a useEffect dependency array isn't a list of "everything this function touches" — it's a list of reactive values the Effect's job depends on. If a value changing should legitimately restart what the Effect is doing, it belongs in the array, full stop; that's not a style choice, it's correctness. But some reads inside an Effect aren't about what the Effect is doing at all — they're about what to do when something the Effect already set up happens later. React 19.2 gives that second category a name — an Effect Event — and a Hook to create one: useEffectEvent.

An Effect Event is a function, declared with useEffectEvent(fn), whose body is deliberately non-reactive: every time your component re-renders, React relinks the function to that render's latest props and state, but the function itself is never a dependency and never forces anything to re-run. You call it from inside an Effect (or from inside another Effect Event) when the thing it does should happen using whatever is current right now, not whatever was current when the Effect last ran.

Put plainly: roomId answers "what should this Effect be connected to?" — that's reactive, and it belongs in the array. theme answers "what should happen, using today's value, when the thing I already connected to does something?" — that's an Effect Event, and it has no business in the array at all.

Stage 1 — the naive fix and its stale closure

Before useEffectEvent existed, the common workaround was to simply drop theme from the array and disable the lint rule:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => {
      // theme is captured from THIS render, forever, until roomId changes again
      showNotification("Connected!", theme);
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
    // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps -- intentionally wrong, see below
  }, [roomId]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

This stops the reconnect. It also freezes theme at whatever it was the moment the Effect last ran. JavaScript closures capture variables by reference to the scope they were created in, not by re-reading them later — so the theme inside connection.on("connected", …) is the one value from the render that created this particular closure. Flip dark mode ten times after that; the notification keeps showing the old theme until roomId changes and the whole Effect reruns. That's the stale closure: the code looks like it reads theme, but it's reading a frozen copy from the past.

This is the trap of "just remove it from the deps array and silence the warning": you've fixed the symptom (unwanted reconnects) by reintroducing the exact class of bug the lint rule exists to prevent (stale reads), just somewhere the rule can no longer see it.

Stage 2 — useEffectEvent, correctly

useEffectEvent splits the two jobs apart explicitly instead of hiding one of them:

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    // Always reads the CURRENT theme, no matter when this runs.
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]); // only roomId — and this time that's actually correct, not a lie

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key concept: onConnected is recreated on every render like any other local function, but calling it never reads a frozen snapshot — React always runs it against the component's latest props and state. Its identity is deliberately not stable across renders (unlike a useState setter or a useCallback-memoized function) — that's by design, so nothing can accidentally rely on it staying the same or pass it around like a normal callback. It simply can never legally appear in the dependency array in the first place, so the instability never causes a re-run. The Effect's dependency array now says something true: this Effect only needs to re-run when roomId changes. theme can change a thousand times without touching the connection, and the notification will still report whatever theme is active the instant it fires.

Toggle dark mode now: no disconnect, no reconnect, and the next notification shows the theme you just switched to. Both halves of the original bug — unwanted reconnects and stale reads — are gone, because they were never actually the same problem. They were two different values wearing one dependency array.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stage 3 — more than one Effect Event

The pattern scales past a single notification. Say the chat room also has a mute toggle that should silence a "ping" sound without, again, reconnecting:

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme, isMuted }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  const onMessage = useEffectEvent((message) => {
    if (!isMuted) playSound();
    logMessage(message, theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.on("message", (msg) => onMessage(msg));
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]); // roomId is the only reactive value here

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key concept: theme and isMuted can each change independently, as often as the user likes, and neither one is a dependency anywhere. The rule that decides what goes in useEffect's array hasn't changed — list every reactive value the Effect's behavior depends on — it's just that theme and isMuted were never one of those to begin with. They were Effect Event inputs all along; useEffectEvent just gives that distinction a real API instead of a lint-rule workaround.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • You can only call an Effect Event from inside an Effect, or from inside another Effect Event. Calling it during render, or handing it to a child component or another Hook as a prop, is not supported — eslint-plugin-react-hooks (6.1 and later; the current major is 7.x) flags both.
  • It must be declared at the top level of a component or custom Hook, like any other Hook — not inside a loop, condition, or nested function. If you need one per item in a list, pull that item into its own component.
  • It cannot go in a dependency array. You don't need to add it — the lint rule never asks you to — and if you add it anyway, a current eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags it directly (Functions returned from useEffectEvent must not be included in the dependency array) and tells you to remove it, because the whole point is that it isn't reactive.
  • It is not a blanket fix for exhaustive-deps warnings. If a value genuinely should restart the Effect — roomId in every example above — wrapping it in useEffectEvent to make the warning go away reintroduces the exact stale-closure bug Stage 1 showed, just with a newer API wrapped around it. The question to ask every time is "should this value actually restart what the Effect is doing?", not "how do I make the warning stop."
  • It doesn't replace useRef for everything. If you need to read a value from outside any Effect at all — say, inside a setTimeout callback registered by an event handler, not an Effect — useEffectEvent's restriction to Effects means a ref, or a plain callback prop, is still the right tool.
  • Server Components never run Effects, so this is purely a client-component concern; it doesn't change anything about the server/client boundary.

Best practices

  • Reach for useEffectEvent when an Effect's trigger condition should stay narrow (one connection per roomId) but an action it fires needs to use whatever is current at the moment it fires, not whatever was current when the Effect last started.
  • Don't reach for it reflexively every time exhaustive-deps complains. First ask whether the flagged value should actually resynchronize the Effect. If yes, keep it in the array — that's not friction, that's the rule doing its job.
  • Keep Effect Events small and named for what they do (onConnected, onMessage), not for what they avoid (stableTheme). The name should describe the moment it fires, because that's the mental model you're encoding.
  • Pair it with a real connection/subscription pattern, not a one-off side effect. The value of splitting reactive setup from non-reactive reaction shows up most in Effects that stay alive across renders — connections, subscriptions, timers — not in an Effect that runs once and is done.

FAQ

Is useEffectEvent a replacement for useCallback?

No. useCallback memoizes a function's identity across renders so a child doesn't re-render or a dependency array doesn't see a "new" function every time. useEffectEvent doesn't memoize for performance — it changes what the function is allowed to see (always-latest, never-reactive) and where it can be called from (only Effects and other Effect Events). They solve different problems and aren't interchangeable.

Can I call an Effect Event from a click handler?

No — an Effect Event can only be called from inside an Effect or another Effect Event, and the lint rule enforces this. If you need current-value behavior inside an onClick, you already have it: a normal event handler always closes over the latest render's values naturally, because it's recreated every render. The stale-closure problem this Hook solves is specific to long-lived Effects, not short-lived event handlers.

Did this exist before React 19.2?

Yes, behind an unstable name. It shipped for a long stretch as experimental_useEffectEvent, and the stabilized, unprefixed useEffectEvent landed in React 19.2 (October 2025). Code written against the experimental name needs the import updated, but the behavior and rules carried over.

Does useEffectEvent need a special ESLint setup?

You need a current eslint-plugin-react-hooks (6.1+; 7.x as of this writing) for the linter to correctly exclude Effect Event functions from dependency-array warnings instead of flagging them as missing. Without it, you'll fight the linter over something it already knows how to handle in a current version.

What happens if I put the Effect Event function in the dependency array anyway?

A current eslint-plugin-react-hooks flags it and tells you to remove it — it won't silently let it through. Functionally, adding it wouldn't do anything useful even if the linter allowed it: the function reference itself isn't what makes the behavior reactive or not. The reactivity question was never about the Effect Event's identity; it's about the values inside it, which are intentionally not tracked.

Cheat sheet

Situation What to do Why
A value decides what the Effect connects to / sets up Keep it in the dependency array It's reactive — the Effect's job changes when it changes
A value is only read after something the Effect set up fires Read it inside a useEffectEvent Always current, never forces a re-run
Tempted to silence exhaustive-deps by deleting a dependency Ask: should this value restart the Effect? If yes, keep it. If no, wrap the code that reads it in useEffectEvent Deleting it silently reintroduces a stale closure
Need current-value behavior inside an onClick/onChange Do nothing special Event handlers already close over the latest render
Need current-value behavior inside a setTimeout set up outside any Effect Use a ref useEffectEvent only works from inside Effects 
import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme, isMuted }) {
  // Non-reactive reads live here — never in the deps array, never the trigger.
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showNotification("Connected!", theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    // Only truly reactive values live here.
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on("connected", () => onConnected());
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]);

  return <h1>Welcome to {roomId}</h1>;
}

Key takeaways

  • A useEffect dependency array lists reactive values the Effect's job depends on — not every value the Effect's body happens to read.
  • Deleting a value from the array to stop an unwanted re-run reintroduces a stale closure: the deleted value gets frozen at whatever it was when the Effect last ran.
  • useEffectEvent (stable since React 19.2, October 2025) gives non-reactive reads a real home: the function always sees the latest props/state, but it's never a dependency and never retriggers the Effect.
  • It can only be called from inside an Effect or another Effect Event — never during render, never passed to a child or another Hook.
  • It is not a workaround for exhaustive-deps — if a value should genuinely resynchronize the Effect, it still belongs in the array.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

That chat room from the opening scene now reconnects exactly when it should — when the room changes — and never when someone just prefers a darker screen. The bug was never really about dark mode; it was two different questions hiding inside one dependency array, and useEffectEvent is what finally lets you answer them separately.

If React Derived State taught you that an Effect syncing one piece of state into another is usually a bug, this is the companion lesson for the Effects you do need: not every value they read is there for the same reason, and now there's a real API for telling them apart. And if Re-render vs Remount taught you that key decides which component instance you're looking at, the same instinct applies here — roomId decides which connection you're looking at, and theme never should have.

Have you shipped a stale-closure bug from an Effect's dependency array — did you find it from a bug report, or from reading the code? Tell me below.

  • React Re-render vs Remount: What Actually Triggers Each

articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Beat Online Discounts & Keep Your Walk-in Customers

A 100% client-side, zero-server competitive pricing intelligence assistant designed specifically for brick-and-mortar retail shop owners.

What I Built

The Problem: Showrooming & Predatory E-Commerce Discounts

Every single day, independent offline store owners (clothing boutiques, electronics & mobile stores, kirana supermarkets, and footwear outlets) face the exact same frustrating scenario:
A customer walks into the physical store, tries on a jacket, inspects a phone, or asks about groceries, pulls out their smartphone, and says:

"I saw this ₹500 cheaper online on Amazon / Flipkart! Can you match the price?"

Most offline shopkeepers panic: they either give in and slash their hard-earned profit margins, or refuse and watch the customer walk straight out the door.

The Solution: PricePulse AI

PricePulse AI is a zero-server, privacy-first competitive intelligence dashboard running 100% inside the shopkeeper's web browser. In under 2 seconds, the store owner can paste any online product link and enter their current shop price.

PricePulse immediately analyzes the competitor listing and equips the shopkeeper with an In-Store Action Plan:

  1. 🎯 Risk to Shop (The Pulse Meter): An animated SVG gauge calculating an instant threat score (0–100) that categorizes whether the competitor move is a negligible online illusion or an aggressive flash sale requiring defensive action.
  2. 📊 Your Shop vs. Competitor (The Diff Matrix): A 4-card transition grid showing where physical retail beats e-commerce:
    • Price Comparison: True delta percentage between in-store price and online listed price.
    • Delivery vs. Instant Take-Home: Comparing courier delays (3–6 days) and hidden handling fees vs. immediate take-home tonight.
    • In-Store Trial & Perks: Hands-on trial room fitting, audio testing, and personal service vs. online return friction.
    • Trust & Warranty: Instant 1-to-1 in-store counter replacement vs. courier return hassles and lost parcels.
  3. 🗣️ Staff Counter-Script (Objection Handler): Word-for-word spoken dialogue for sales assistants to counter "I saw it cheaper online" objections confidently on the spot.
  4. 💬 WhatsApp Customer Broadcast: Engaging, high-converting messages with emojis tailored for the store's VIP broadcast list or WhatsApp Status.
  5. 📋 Shop Counter Signboard: High-impact text ready to print on an A4 sheet for checkout counters, fitting rooms, or chalkboard easels.
  6. 🎁 In-Store Margin Bundle & Playbook: Smart accessory add-ons and value shields that close walk-ins without sacrificing product margins.

Who Would Pay For It?

  • Independent Retail Store Owners: Boutique clothing shops, mobile/laptop retail stores, consumer electronics dealers, optical stores, and neighborhood kiranas.
  • Retail Store Managers & Franchises: Multi-branch retailers needing standardized staff counter-scripts so sales staff don't give unauthorized cash discounts.
  • Commercial Viability: As a $12/month or $99/year micro-SaaS, or bundled as a one-time digital kit for local retail associations. Because it runs 100% client-side, the operational hosting cost is $0.00, making gross margins near 100%.

Demo

  • Live Web App: https://ujjwalgupta2021.github.io/PricePulse-AI/ (Deployable to GitHub Pages with 0 server configuration)
  • Built-in Interactive Demos (Zero Setup Required): Clicking any demo button instantly simulates real retail defense scenarios without requiring an API key:
    • 👕 Clothing Boutique: Arctic Expedition Parka vs. discount e-commerce apparel seller.
    • 📱 Mobile & Electronics: Noise-Cancelling Wireless Headphones vs. online tech marketplace.
    • 🛒 Supermarket / Kirana: Premium Basmati Rice & Oil Combo vs. quick-commerce delivery apps.
  • Theme Switcher: Full support for both Dark Glassmorphic Theme and clean, high-contrast Light Retail Theme.

Code

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ujjwalgupta2021/PricePulse-AI
  • Core Architecture:
    • index.html — Clean semantic structure, SVG gauge meters, and accessibility-first modal views.
    • styles.css — Modern glassmorphism system with CSS custom properties, responsive grids, and dark/light modes.
    • js/app.js — Application lifecycle, event orchestration, and markdown export engine.
    • js/gemini.js — Direct HTTPS connection to Google Gemini Flash with automatic model negotiation and resilient JSON parsing.
    • js/scraper.js — Client-side scraping bridge cascading across Jina Reader AI, AllOrigins, and URL slug anti-bot extractors.
    • js/pulse-meter.js — High-performance SVG needle rotation and stroke-dashoffset animation.
    • js/diff-matrix.js — High-contrast side-by-side transition cards comparing baseline vs. live page data.
    • js/counter-attack.js — Multi-tab action plan generator with 1-click clipboard copy.
    • js/storage.js — 100% client-side LocalStorage vault for private keys, preferences, and watchlist.

How I Built It

1. Pure Open-Innovation & Client-Side Agent Harness

PricePulse AI was built without any backend servers, Python microservices, or node daemons. The entire application runs directly inside the client's browser as a zero-server agent harness:

  • Vanilla HTML5 & CSS3: No bloated CSS frameworks or heavyweight JavaScript bundles; initial load takes < 150ms.
  • Client-Side Scraping Bridge: Directly reads competitor product listings using Jina Reader AI (https://r.jina.ai/), AllOrigins proxy, and an intelligent URL slug parser with Amazon/Flipkart anti-bot detection.
  • Open-Weight & Model-Agnostic Architecture: Built around the open HTTP standard for generative inference. While it pairs natively with Google Gemini Flash for speed (<600ms), its modular schema engine is compatible with open-weight models (including Google Gemma 2B/9B, Llama 3, and Mistral via local WebLLM or Ollama proxies).

2. Google Gemini Flash Integration with Dynamic Model Auto-Negotiation

PricePulse connects directly to Google AI Studio's Gemini Flash REST API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta):

  • Automated Catalog Discovery: The engine queries ModelService.ListModels to dynamically discover supported models on the user's key (gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-3.8-flash) without requiring confusing manual dropdown configuration.
  • Strict Schema Steering: Uses official system instructions with JSON response constraints to ensure high-fidelity retail defense outputs.
  • Resilient JSON Parser: Employs regex { ... } substring recovery to gracefully extract valid data even if the model outputs conversational text.
  • Fail-Safe Retail Intelligence Shield: If the AI API experiences network disconnects or quota rate limits, PricePulse automatically activates an offline synthesized retail audit using the real URL, extracted product title, and store baseline, ensuring 0% crash rate.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  1. Zero Recurring Overhead for Mom-and-Pop Retailers:

    Most commercial retail software costs $50–$200/month because of cloud servers, databases, and middleman APIs. By utilizing open web standards, free-tier client-side AI, and static hosting, offline store owners can access enterprise-grade competitive intelligence without paying hefty SaaS subscriptions.

  2. Absolute Privacy of Store Margins & Wholesale Pricing:

    Local shopkeepers will never upload their private wholesale margins, supplier costs, or pricing baseline to a closed, centralized cloud database where competitor algorithms could scrape or exploit it. In PricePulse AI, every price check and API key stays sealed in the browser's local sandbox (localStorage).

  3. No Vendor Lock-In:

    The application does not depend on a single proprietary backend. If an API endpoint changes, the open architecture adapts dynamically or runs client-side simulation.

My Agent Session

This project was developed with Google Antigravity AI as an advanced agentic coding partner.

Key milestones achieved during the session:

  • Designed and refined the Retail Defense Pivot: Transitioned technical e-commerce scraping jargon into actionable spoken dialogue for offline retail shopkeepers.
  • Engineered the High-Speed Connection & Auto-Negotiation Engine: Eliminated slow sequential pinging and built dynamic Google Gemini catalog discovery.
  • Solved Anti-Bot Interception for Amazon.in: Built smart URL slug parsers to extract real product names directly from /product-name/dp/ASIN links even when target sites throw robot checks.
  • Enhanced Typography & Accessibility: Designed a high-contrast Light Theme alongside the Dark Mode to guarantee clear visibility under bright store counter lighting.

Prize Categories

  • Primary Track: Side Hustle (Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2)
  • Partner Categories:
    • Best Use of AI / Gemini API
    • Zero-Server Open-Source Web Application

articles.title: Screenshot Every Page of a Website from Its Sitemap with One Node.js Script
articles.description: Read every URL from a sitemap, capture each page at desktop and mobile widths in real Chrome, and save named PNGs, a CSV manifest and a contact sheet with one Node.js script.
articles.body_html:
You're about to relaunch a site and someone asks for a screenshot of every page as it stands today. Or a client wants to sign off 140 pages of copy, or legal wants a dated record of what the pricing page said. Doing it by hand means opening each URL, waiting for the lazy images, closing the cookie banner and saving the file under a name you'll still understand next month. Two minutes a page adds up to most of a working day for a 200-page site.

So I wrote one Node.js script that reads the sitemap, captures every page at desktop and mobile widths in real Chrome, and leaves a folder of named PNGs, a CSV manifest and a contact sheet. Last run: 38 full-page captures in 35 seconds, no failures.

Disclosure: I run HTML to Image, and the script uses its Screenshot API for the captures. This is a cross-post of the full guide on the HTML to Image blog, which is the canonical version and goes further into webhooks, costs and compliance archives.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18 or later, for the built-in fetch.
  • An HTML to Image API key. The free credits are enough to try this on a handful of pages.
  • A site with a sitemap, or a text file of URLs from a crawl. 
npm install @html2img/client
export HTML2IMG_API_KEY=your_api_key

Step 1: Find the sitemap

Most sites declare their sitemap in robots.txt, so check there first:

curl -s https://example.com/robots.txt | grep -i '^sitemap:'

If nothing comes back, try /sitemap.xml, then /sitemap_index.xml (Yoast and Rank Math on WordPress), then /wp-sitemap.xml (WordPress core since 5.5). Big sites use a sitemap index that points at child sitemaps, some of them gzipped. The script follows all of that, so you only ever pass the top-level URL.

One caveat: a sitemap is the list the CMS chooses to publish. Orphaned landing pages and anything marked noindex won't be in it. For a migration archive, cross-check against a crawl and feed the script a text file instead.

Step 2: The script

Save this as capture-site.mjs. It's long-ish because it handles the boring parts properly: sitemap indexes, .gz files, duplicates, a credit check before spending anything, four captures at a time, retries for errors that can recover, and the reports at the end.

// capture-site.mjs
// node capture-site.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml [--dry-run]
// node capture-site.mjs urls.txt
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { gunzipSync } from 'node:zlib';
import {
  Html2img,
  InsufficientCreditsError,
  TimeoutError,
  ServerError,
  ConnectionError,
} from '@html2img/client';

const SOURCE = process.argv[2];
const DRY_RUN = process.argv.includes('--dry-run');
const OUT = 'shots';
const CONCURRENCY = 4;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;

// One credit per page per variant.
const VARIANTS = [
  { name: 'desktop', width: 1440 },
  { name: 'mobile', width: 390 },
  // { name: 'pdf', format: 'pdf' }, // A4 document with a real text layer
];

// Sent with every capture.
const CAPTURE = {
  fullpage: true,
  css: `#onetrust-banner-sdk, .onetrust-pc-dark-filter, #CybotCookiebotDialog,
        .qc-cmp2-container, .osano-cm-window, #cookie-law-info-bar,
        .intercom-frame, #crisp-chatbox { display: none !important; }`,
};

const SKIP = /\.(pdf|jpe?g|png|gif|webp|svg|zip|mp4|xml)$/i;
const apiKey = process.env.HTML2IMG_API_KEY;
const client = DRY_RUN ? null : new Html2img(apiKey);

// 1. Every <loc> in a sitemap, following sitemap indexes and .gz files.
async function readSitemap(url, seen = new Set()) {
  if (seen.has(url)) return [];
  seen.add(url);
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} returned ${res.status}`);
  let body = Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer());
  if (body[0] === 0x1f && body[1] === 0x8b) body = gunzipSync(body);
  const xml = body.toString('utf8');
  const locs = [...xml.matchAll(/<loc>\s*(?:<!\[CDATA\[)?(.*?)(?:\]\]>)?\s*<\/loc>/gs)]
    .map((m) => m[1].replace(/&(amp|apos|quot|lt|gt);/g, (_, e) =>
      ({ amp: '&', apos: "'", quot: '"', lt: '<', gt: '>' })[e]));
  if (!/<sitemapindex[\s>]/.test(xml)) return locs;
  const children = await Promise.all(locs.map((loc) => readSitemap(loc, seen)));
  return children.flat();
}

// 2. Same site only, no files, no duplicates.
const bare = (host) => host.replace(/^www\./, '');
function toPages(urls, onlyHost) {
  const pages = new Set();
  for (const raw of urls) {
    let u;
    try { u = new URL(raw.trim()); } catch { continue; } // header rows, blanks
    if (onlyHost && bare(u.hostname) !== bare(onlyHost)) continue;
    if (SKIP.test(u.pathname)) continue;
    u.hash = '';
    pages.add(u.href);
  }
  return [...pages];
}

// "/blog/launch-notes/" -> "blog__launch-notes"
let multiSite = false;
function fileName(page) {
  const { hostname, pathname, search } = new URL(page);
  const slug = (pathname + search)
    .replace(/^\/+|\/+$/g, '')
    .split('/')
    .map((part) => part.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/gi, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, ''))
    .join('__')
    .toLowerCase()
    .slice(0, 150) || 'home';
  return multiSite ? `${bare(hostname)}__${slug}` : slug;
}

async function creditsLeft() {
  const res = await fetch('https://app.html2img.com/api/me', {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': apiKey },
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Key check failed with ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()).credits_remaining;
}

const retryable = (err) =>
  err instanceof TimeoutError ||
  err instanceof ServerError ||
  err instanceof ConnectionError ||
  err.errorCode === 'page_load_timeout';

// 3. One capture, retried on errors that are worth a second attempt.
async function capture({ page, variant }) {
  const { name, ...options } = variant;
  const ext = options.format === 'pdf' ? 'pdf' : 'png';
  const row = { page, variant: name, status: 'failed', file: '', image_url: '', error: '' };
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
      const shot = await client.screenshot({ url: page, ...CAPTURE, ...options });
      row.image_url = shot.url;
      const img = await fetch(shot.url);
      if (!img.ok) throw new Error(`download returned ${img.status}`);
      row.file = `${name}/${fileName(page)}.${ext}`;
      await writeFile(`${OUT}/${row.file}`, Buffer.from(await img.arrayBuffer()));
      return { ...row, status: 'ok', error: '' };
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof InsufficientCreditsError) throw err;
      row.error = err.errorCode ?? err.message;
      if (!retryable(err) || attempt === MAX_ATTEMPTS) return row;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 3000 * attempt));
    }
  }
}

// 4. A fixed number of captures in flight at once.
async function runAll(jobs) {
  const rows = [];
  let next = 0;
  let stopped = false;
  async function lane() {
    while (!stopped && next < jobs.length) {
      const job = jobs[next++];
      try {
        const row = await capture(job);
        rows.push(row);
        console.log(`${rows.length}/${jobs.length} ${row.status} ${row.variant} ${job.page}`);
      } catch (err) {
        if (!stopped) console.error(`Stopping early: ${err.message}`);
        stopped = true;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: CONCURRENCY }, lane));
  return rows;
}

// 5. A manifest for spreadsheets and an index.html for people.
async function writeReports(rows) {
  const cols = ['page', 'variant', 'status', 'file', 'image_url', 'error'];
  const cell = (v) => `"${String(v).replaceAll('"', '""')}"`;
  const csv = [cols, ...rows.map((r) => cols.map((c) => r[c]))]
    .map((line) => line.map(cell).join(','))
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/manifest.csv`, csv);

  const esc = (s) => s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, (c) => `&#${c.charCodeAt(0)};`);
  const cards = rows
    .filter((r) => r.status === 'ok' && r.file.endsWith('.png'))
    .map((r) => `<a href="${esc(r.file)}"><img src="${esc(r.file)}" loading="lazy"><span>${r.variant} · ${esc(r.page)}</span></a>`)
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/index.html`, `<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Site capture</title>
<style>body{font:14px system-ui;margin:24px;display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:20px}
a{color:#334155;text-decoration:none}img{width:100%;height:320px;object-fit:cover;object-position:top;border:1px solid #e2e6ec;border-radius:8px}
span{display:block;margin-top:6px;word-break:break-all}</style>\n${cards}`);
}

const fromSitemap = /^https?:\/\//.test(SOURCE);
const urls = fromSitemap
  ? await readSitemap(SOURCE)
  : (await readFile(SOURCE, 'utf8')).split(/\r?\n/);
const pages = toPages(urls, fromSitemap ? new URL(SOURCE).hostname : null);
multiSite = new Set(pages.map((page) => bare(new URL(page).hostname))).size > 1;

if (DRY_RUN) {
  console.log(pages.join('\n'));
  process.exit(0);
}

const jobs = pages.flatMap((page) => VARIANTS.map((variant) => ({ page, variant })));
const credits = await creditsLeft();
console.log(`${pages.length} pages x ${VARIANTS.length} variants = ${jobs.length} credits. Balance: ${credits}.`);
if (credits < jobs.length) {
  console.error('Not enough credits for the whole run. Trim the list or top up first.');
  process.exit(1);
}

for (const { name } of VARIANTS) await mkdir(`${OUT}/${name}`, { recursive: true });
const rows = await runAll(jobs);
await writeReports(rows);

const failed = rows.filter((r) => r.status !== 'ok').length;
const skipped = jobs.length - rows.length;
console.log(`Saved ${rows.length - failed}, failed ${failed}, skipped ${skipped}. Open ${OUT}/index.html`);

The css string is doing quiet but important work. The renderer arrives as a first-time visitor with no cookies, so every page shows its consent banner. Injecting display: none !important for the common consent providers and chat widgets takes them out before the shot. If a site uses something else, find the banner's ID in dev tools and add it.

Step 3: Dry run first, then capture

--dry-run prints the URLs the script would capture. It doesn't need a key and spends nothing, so use it to filter out tag archives, paginated listings and anything else you don't need a picture of:

node capture-site.mjs https://html2img.com/sitemap.xml --dry-run | grep '/tools/' > urls.txt
node capture-site.mjs urls.txt

That's the real run I mentioned at the top, against the free tools section of my own site:

19 pages x 2 variants = 38 credits. Balance: 100.
1/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
2/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
3/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/
4/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/tools/
...
38/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/youtube-thumbnail/
Saved 38, failed 0, skipped 0. Open shots/index.html

Spot the first line. My lazy grep also matched /docs/mcp/tools/, which I never meant to include. That's exactly why the dry run exists: grep '^https://html2img.com/tools/' would have kept it out.

The desktop captures came back 1,440 pixels wide and between 3,737 and 10,016 pixels tall. Here's the index.html the run produced, each card cropped to the top of its page:

What the script does when things go wrong

Not every page cooperates, so the retry logic only retries what a second attempt can fix:

  • 504 timeouts, 500s, slow-loading sites and dropped connections get two more attempts, 3 then 6 seconds apart.
  • Dead links, SSL failures and sites that block automated visitors (url_not_found, url_unreachable, connection_refused) are logged in manifest.csv and skipped.
  • Running out of credits stops every lane, still writes the reports, and tells you how many captures were skipped.

To re-run only the failures, pull them out of the manifest and run them in a fresh folder so the first run's reports stay intact:

awk -F'","' '$3 == "failed" { print substr($1, 2) }' shots/manifest.csv | sort -u > retry.txt
mkdir retry && cd retry && node ../capture-site.mjs ../retry.txt

Keep CONCURRENCY low for sites you don't own. Every capture is a real page load against somebody's production server.

A few limits worth planning around

  • Public pages only. The renderer has no cookies or headers, so anything behind a login captures as the sign-in page.
  • Infinite scroll has no bottom. Cap the feed with injected CSS such as main.feed { max-height: 12000px; overflow: hidden; }.
  • Closed accordions stay closed. Nobody clicks during a capture, so open hidden panels with CSS if they matter.
  • One credit per page per width. Desktop plus mobile doubles the cost, and the PDF variant adds a third.

Where I'd use this

Before a migration, so you have the old site on disk the day the DNS switches. For client sign-off, where one contact sheet beats 200 links. And for compliance, where the commented-out pdf variant gives you searchable A4 documents in a dated folder.

The full guide on the HTML to Image blog also covers handing long captures to a webhook instead of waiting on them, a bash version for short URL lists, and what a full-site capture costs at different sizes.

How are you archiving sites before a relaunch at the moment? Browser extension, Screaming Frog, something homegrown? Let me know in the comments.
